train.title: BUG: segfault on next() after a chunked read_csv chunk raised (C engine)
train.body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import io

import pandas as pd

# column "b" has one non-numeric token, so converting the first chunk raises
data = "a,b\n" + "".join(f"{i},{'oops' if i == 5 else i}\n" for i in range(20))

reader = pd.read_csv(io.StringIO(data), dtype={"b": "int64"}, chunksize=10)

try:
    next(reader)
except ValueError:
    pass  # invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'oops'

next(reader)  # <-- segfault
```

### Issue Description

If converting a chunk raises, the `TextFileReader` is left in a state where the
next `next()` / `get_chunk()` call segfaults instead of raising.

The exception from the first chunk is the expected one:

```
ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'oops'
```

The second call crashes the interpreter. `faulthandler` puts it inside the
Cython `TextReader.read` call:

```
Fatal Python error: Segmentation fault

Current thread 0x00000001d8f81c40 (most recent call first):
  File ".../pandas/io/parsers/c_parser_wrapper.py", line 234 in read
  File ".../pandas/io/parsers/readers.py", line 1923 in read
  File ".../pandas/io/parsers/readers.py", line 1985 in get_chunk
  File ".../pandas/io/parsers/readers.py", line 1843 in __next__
```

Scope, from varying the reproducer (identical results on 3.0.5 and 2.3.3):

| variant | result |
| --- | --- |
| `engine="c"`, `chunksize=10` | **segfault** |
| `engine="c"`, `iterator=True` + `get_chunk(10)` | **segfault** |
| `engine="c"`, `converters=` raising on row 5 instead of `dtype=` | **segfault** |
| `engine="python"`, `chunksize=10` | raises `ValueError`, no crash |
| `engine="c"`, no `dtype=` (first chunk does not raise) | fine |

So it is specific to the C parser, and what sets it up is that a chunk raised
during conversion — `dtype=` is just a convenient way to trigger that, and a
raising `converters=` callable does it too.

Not a regression: reproduces identically on 3.0.5, on 2.3.3, and on a source
build of current `main`. Nothing string- or pyarrow-specific is involved — the
reproducer has no string column.

### Expected Behavior

The second `next(reader)` should either raise a Python-level exception or return
the remaining rows. Crashing the interpreter is never acceptable, and it is
particularly bad here because catching a per-chunk conversion error and
continuing is a natural pattern for a chunked read.

train.title: DOC: "10 minutes to pandas" guide doesn't explain that double brackets return a DataFrame, not a Series
train.body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that the issue still exists on the latest versions of the docs on `main` [here](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/)


### Location of the documentation

https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/user_guide/10min.html#getitem

### Documentation problem

The "Getitem ([])" section of the "10 minutes to pandas" tutorial shows that a single label in brackets will return a Series:
```
df["A"]
```
It also shows that a list of multiple labels returns a DataFrame:
```
df[["B", "A"]]
```

It never shows the specific case of a list containing a single label (e.g. `df[["A"]]`, which also returns a DataFrame). However, since `df["A"]` and `df[["A"]]` look nearly identical but return different object types, this could be a common point of confusion for beginners, yet isn't directly illustrated anywhere on this page. The distinction is already covered in the more comprehensive "[Indexing and selecting data](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/user_guide/indexing.html#basics)" guide, but it is not mentioned in the "10 minutes to pandas" tutorial, where many new users will actually first encounter column selection.

### Suggested fix for documentation

Add a short note and example directly after the existing `df[["B", "A"]]` example, describing `df[["A"]]` and stating that it returns a DataFrame containing that one column, rather than a Series.

I would like to work on this myself, and plan submit a PR with the fix.

train.body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the main branch of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

columns = pd.MultiIndex.from_product(
    [["A", "B"], ["c", "d"], ["e", "f"]], names=["l0", "l1", "l2"]
)
df = pd.DataFrame(np.arange(8).reshape(1, 8), columns=columns)

df.stack([0, 0])        # AssertionError, with no message
df.stack(["l0", "l0"])  # AssertionError, with no message
df.stack([1, -2])       # AssertionError, with no message
df.stack([2, -1])       # IndexError: pop index out of range
```

### Issue Description

Passing a `level` list that contains duplicate entries to `DataFrame.stack` fails with an
internal error instead of a user-facing one:

```
  File "pandas/core/reshape/reshape.py", line 1023, in stack_v3
    assert isinstance(stack_cols, MultiIndex)
AssertionError
```

`stack_v3` computes the columns to stack from the deduplicated `set(level)`:

```python
set_levels = set(level)
stack_cols = frame.columns._drop_level_numbers(
    [k for k in range(frame.columns.nlevels - 1, -1, -1) if k not in set_levels]
)
```

but later branches on the length of the original, non-deduplicated list:

```python
if len(level) > 1:
    sorter = np.argsort(level)
    assert isinstance(stack_cols, MultiIndex)
```

With `level=[0, 0]`, `set_levels` has one entry, so `stack_cols` is a plain `Index`, while
`len(level)` is still 2 and the assertion fires.

Note that the duplicates need not be written literally. `DataFrame.stack` resolves level
names and negative level numbers with `_get_level_number` before reaching `stack_v3`, so on
3-level columns `["l0", "l0"]`, `[1, -2]` and `[2, -1]` all normalize to duplicated level
numbers and hit the same code path.

This is also a change in behavior from the previous implementation, which accepted duplicate
levels and stacked sequentially:

```python
>>> df.stack([0, 0], future_stack=False)  # legacy implementation
l2       e  f
  l0 l1
0 A  c   1  2
     d   3  4
  B  c   5  6
     d   7  8

>>> df.stack(0).stack(0)  # identical result
```

### Expected Behavior

An informative exception rather than a bare `AssertionError` or an `IndexError` from an
internal `list.pop`.

There are two defensible behaviors, so I wanted to raise it rather than pick one silently:

1. **Raise an informative `ValueError`.** The current implementation stacks the specified
   original column levels simultaneously, and "the same level twice" has no meaning in that
   model. `stack_v3` already raises `ValueError("Columns with duplicate values are not
   supported in stack")` for the analogous duplicate-column case. This also avoids silently
   choosing semantics that differ from the legacy implementation, which stacked two distinct
   levels for `[0, 0]`.
2. **Deduplicate**, so that `stack([0, 0])` behaves as `stack([0])`. This would match the
   sibling APIs, which all accept duplicate levels today: `unstack([0, 0])`,
   `groupby(level=[0, 0])`, `droplevel([0, 0])` and `reorder_levels` all succeed. The
   downside is that it silently changes the legacy result rather than flagging it.

I have a PR ready implementing option 1, following the precedent of #25413, where `concat`
with `keys` was changed to raise an informative `ValueError` instead of an `AssertionError`.
Happy to switch it to option 2 if maintainers prefer consistency with `unstack`.

### Installed Versions

<details>

Built from source at current `main` (1b1e271f30b3ac77a051dc8293294d7b526db87e), Python 3.13.1,
NumPy 2.5.1, Windows 11 (x86_64, MSVC build).

</details>

train.title: BUG: read_excel(engine="odf") ignores office:value on <table:covered-table-cell>
train.body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd
from odf.opendocument import OpenDocumentSpreadsheet
from odf.table import CoveredTableCell, Table, TableCell, TableRow

path = Path("covered_cell_value.ods")

doc = OpenDocumentSpreadsheet()
sheet = Table(name="Sheet1")
doc.spreadsheet.addElement(sheet)

row0 = TableRow()
sheet.addElement(row0)
row0.addElement(TableCell(valuetype="float", value="1"))
row0.addElement(TableCell(valuetype="float", value="100"))

# A covered cell carrying its own explicit office:value/office:value-type —
# this is exactly what the cells covered by an ODF array/matrix formula
# (table:number-matrix-rows-spanned) hold, per the OpenDocument spec.
row1 = TableRow()
sheet.addElement(row1)
row1.addElement(CoveredTableCell(valuetype="float", value="42"))
row1.addElement(TableCell(valuetype="float", value="200"))

doc.save(str(path))

print(pd.read_excel(path, engine="odf", header=None))
print(pd.read_excel(path, engine="calamine", header=None))


Output:


     0    1
0  1.0  100
1  NaN  200      # engine="odf": the covered cell's value (42) is silently dropped

    0    1
0   1  100
1  42  200       # engine="calamine": reads the same file correctly


(LibreOffice shows correctly the number 42 when opening the file manually.)
```

### Issue Description

`read_excel(engine="odf")` treats every `<table:covered-table-cell>` as empty,
without ever inspecting whether it carries its own `office:value`/
`office:value-type`. The relevant code, in
`pandas/io/excel/_odfreader.py`, `ODFReader.get_sheet_data`:

```python
if sheet_cell.qname == table_cell_name:
    value = self._get_cell_value(sheet_cell)
else:
    value = self.empty_value
```

Any cell that isn't literally a `<table:table-cell>` — i.e. any
`<table:covered-table-cell>` — takes the `else` branch and is hard-coded to
`self.empty_value`, regardless of its actual attributes.

This is usually harmless, since a covered cell is normally just a
merged-away placeholder for an ordinary row/column span with no value of its
own. But it's incorrect for the cells covered by an ODF **array/matrix
formula** (`table:number-matrix-rows-spanned` /
`table:number-matrix-columns-spanned`, [OpenDocument v1.2 Part 1, §9.1.5
`<table:covered-table-cell>`](https://docs.oasis-open.org/office/v1.2/os/OpenDocument-v1.2-os-part1.html#__RefHeading__1415592_253892949);
the attribute itself is defined in §19.680, cross-referenced e.g. in
[MS-OODF3](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/openspecs/office_standards/ms-oodf3/b8bed28a-0722-4814-9e7d-2611229f5eee)):
per the OpenDocument spec, those covered cells hold their own evaluated
result, and real spreadsheet applications (verified with LibreOffice:
`soffice --headless --convert-to csv` recomputes and exports the correct
distinct value for each covered cell) read/recompute them accordingly.

I've confirmed the data is genuinely present and correctly parsed at the
odfpy layer (which pandas' odf engine is built on) — reading the same file
with `odfpy` directly via `cell.getAttrNS(office_ns, "value")` returns `"42"`
for the covered cell — so this is specific to pandas' reader wrapper, not to
odfpy or to how the file was written.


### Expected Behavior

`read_excel(engine="odf")` should read a covered cell's own `office:value`/
`office:value-type` when present, the same way `engine="calamine"` already
does, instead of unconditionally treating it as empty. At minimum, a covered
cell that carries an explicit `office:value` should not silently lose it.


### Installed Versions

```

train.title: DOC: rename_categories dict example is a no-op in categorical.rst
train.body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that the issue still exists on the latest versions of the docs on `main` [here](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/)


### Location of the documentation

[https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/user_guide/categorical.html#renaming-categories](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/user_guide/categorical.html#renaming-categories)

### Documentation problem

The "Renaming categories" example's dict-based rename step silently does
nothing. Current code:
```
s = pd.Series(["a", "b", "c", "a"], dtype="category")
s
new_categories = ["Group %s" % g for g in s.cat.categories]
s = s.cat.rename_categories(new_categories)
s
# You can also pass a dict-like object to map the renaming
s = s.cat.rename_categories({1: "x", 2: "y", 3: "z"})
s
```
By the time the dict-rename line runs, s's categories are already
["Group a", "Group b", "Group c"] (strings), not 1/2/3.
Categorical.rename_categories with a dict only renames keys present in
the current categories and leaves everything else unchanged, so
{1: "x", 2: "y", 3: "z"} matches nothing -- the dict-rename example is a
no-op. The printed output after it is identical to the line before it,
which doesn't demonstrate dict-based renaming at all.

### Suggested fix for documentation

Change the dict keys to match the categories that actually exist at that
point in the example:
```
# You can also pass a dict-like object to map the renaming
s = s.cat.rename_categories({"Group a": "x", "Group b": "y", "Group c": "z"})
s
```
This is a minimal one-line fix and makes the dict-rename example actually
rename something, matching what the comment claims. Verified locally:
after this change the output is Categories (3, str): ['x', 'y', 'z']
instead of an unchanged ['Group a', 'Group b', 'Group c'].

train.title: BUG: datetimelike arithmetic landing on the NaT sentinel silently returns NaT
train.body:
### Summary

`NaT` is stored as `INT64_MIN`, so any datetimelike arithmetic whose result lands exactly on
`INT64_MIN` is indistinguishable from a missing value once stored. `@cython.overflowcheck(True)`
catches a sum that goes *below* `INT64_MIN` but not one that lands *on* it, so there is a
one-step hole at the bottom of the range: the step further out raises, the step onto the
sentinel silently returns `NaT`.

GH-66510 / GH-66520 closed this for parsing and construction. It is still open across
arithmetic, and it is not a single site — it recurs everywhere pandas does datetimelike
addition, and in a few places as a bare `assert` rather than a silent `NaT`.

### Reproducible examples

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from pandas import Period, PeriodDtype, Timedelta, Timestamp
from pandas._libs.tslibs import iNaT

# 1. scalar Timestamp: one step out raises, landing on the sentinel does not
Timestamp.min - Timedelta(1, "ns")     # -> NaT
Timestamp.min - Timedelta(2, "ns")     # -> OutOfBoundsDatetime

# 2. same for the array forms
pd.DatetimeIndex([Timestamp.min]) - Timedelta(1, "ns")   # -> [NaT]
pd.DatetimeIndex([Timestamp.min]) - Timedelta(2, "ns")   # -> OverflowError

# 3. Timestamp +/- ndarray[timedelta64] wraps on the promotion to the finer unit
Timestamp("2500-01-01").as_unit("s") + np.array([1], "m8[ns]")   # -> 1915-06-14
# ... and in the addition itself
Timestamp("2000-01-01") + np.array([9 * 10**18], "m8[ns]")       # -> 1700-08-23

# 4. Timestamp - Timestamp trips a bare assert. Under `python -O` the assert
#    vanishes and you get a Timedelta whose _value is iNaT but which is not NaT,
#    and for which isna() is False.
Timestamp(iNaT + 1) - Timestamp(1)     # -> AssertionError
Timestamp(iNaT + 1) - Timestamp(2)     # -> OutOfBoundsDatetime("Result is too large...")

# 5. Timedelta, scalar and array
Timedelta.min - Timedelta(1, "ns")                  # -> NaT
Timedelta.min + np.array([-1], "m8[ns]")            # -> [NaT]
Timedelta(1, "ns") * (-(2**63))                     # -> AssertionError
Timedelta(1, "ns") * np.array([-(2**63)])           # -> [NaT]

# 6. Period ordinals
per = Period._from_ordinal(iNaT + 1, PeriodDtype("ns"))
per - 1                                             # -> NaT
per - Timedelta(1, "ns")                            # -> NaT

# 7. vectorized offsets
pd.Series([Timestamp(iNaT + 1)]) + pd.offsets.DateOffset(nanoseconds=-1)   # -> NaT
pd.DatetimeIndex([Timestamp(iNaT + 7 * 86400 * 10**9)]) + pd.offsets.Week(-1)      # -> [NaT]
pd.DatetimeIndex([Timestamp(iNaT + 86400 * 10**9)]) + pd.offsets.BusinessDay(-1)   # -> [NaT]
```

### Expected behavior

A result landing on the sentinel should raise, the same way the step further out of bounds
already does. `NaT` should come back only when an operand was actually missing.

### Inventory

Everything below reaches the sentinel. Grouped by mechanism, since the fix differs.

**Scalar paths that return `NaT`**
- `_Timestamp.__add__` with a timedelta-like (`timestamps.pyx`)
- `_binary_op_method_timedeltalike` — an explicit `if res == NPY_NAT: return NaT`, with a
  standing `TODO: more generally could do an overflowcheck in op?` (`timedeltas.pyx`)
- `Period._add_timedeltalike_scalar`, `Period._add_offset`, and the integer branch of
  `Period.__add__` — all three build an ordinal and hand it to the `Period` constructor, which
  renders `iNaT` as `NaT` (`period.pyx`)

**Scalar paths that trip a bare `assert`**
- `_Timestamp.__sub__` with another `Timestamp`, and `Timedelta` `*` / `/` — both land on
  `assert value != NPY_NAT` in `_timedelta_from_value_and_reso`. This is the worst of the set:
  under `python -O` it produces a live object whose `_value` is `iNaT` but which is not `NaT`
  and for which `isna()` returns `False`.

**Array paths that return `NaT`**
- `add_overflowsafe` (`np_datetime.pyx`), which covers `DatetimeArray`/`TimedeltaArray`/
  `PeriodArray` add and subtract, and so `DatetimeIndex`/`TimedeltaIndex`/`PeriodIndex`/`Series`

train.title: BUG: datetimelike arithmetic landing on the NaT sentinel returns NaT, plus float64 precision loss in timedelta64 arithmetic/reductions
train.body:
Follow-up to GH-66510 / GH-66520, which fixed the *parsing and construction* half of the "value lands on the `NaT` sentinel" problem (`parsers.pyx`, `conversion.pyx`, `strptime.pyx`, `Timestamp.replace`). The *arithmetic* half is still open, and while investigating it I found an adjacent family of `float64` precision bugs in `timedelta64` arithmetic and reductions.

All reproducers below are against `082e77392bd` (main as of 2026-07-29).

Two distinct root causes, filed together because they were found together and overlap in the code they touch — happy to split into separate issues if that's easier to triage.

---

## 1. `NPY_NAT` is `int64.min`, so arithmetic landing on it silently becomes `NaT`

A computed value equal to `NPY_NAT` is perfectly representable in `int64`, but is indistinguishable from `NaT` once stored. Today it is silently read back as `NaT` rather than raising. This affects scalars and arrays across all four datetimelike types.

The scalar and vectorized paths also disagree about *which* error to raise one step further out, so you can't paper over it with a `try/except`.

```python
import pandas as pd
from pandas import Timedelta, Timestamp
from pandas.core.dtypes.dtypes import PeriodDtype

# one ns past the bound -> NaT; two ns past -> raises
Timedelta.min - Timedelta(1, "ns")                  # NaT          <- should raise
Timedelta.min - Timedelta(2, "ns")                  # OverflowError

pd.array([Timedelta.min]) - Timedelta(1, "ns")      # <TimedeltaArray> [NaT]   <- should raise

Timestamp.min.as_unit("ns") - Timedelta(1, "ns")    # NaT          <- should raise
pd.to_datetime([Timestamp.min]).as_unit("ns") - Timedelta(1, "ns")
                                                    # DatetimeIndex(['NaT'])   <- should raise

per = pd.Period._from_ordinal(-(2**63) + 1, PeriodDtype("ns"))
per - 1                                             # NaT          <- should raise
pd.PeriodIndex([per]) - 1                           # PeriodIndex(['NaT'])     <- should raise
```

Notes on the vectorized side: `mul_overflowsafe` got an explicit sentinel check in GH-43178 / GH-65515, but `add_overflowsafe` never did — which is why the `timedelta64`, `datetime64` and Period-ordinal array paths above all still return `NaT`.

### 1b. The same condition surfaces as a message-less `AssertionError`

`_timedelta_from_value_and_reso` guards with a bare `assert value != NPY_NAT`, so a user hitting this gets an `AssertionError` with no message (and nothing at all under `python -O`):

```python
Timestamp.min - Timestamp(1)      # AssertionError:
Timedelta(2, "ns") * (-(2**62))   # AssertionError:
```

---

## 2. `float64` precision loss in `timedelta64` arithmetic and reductions

Separate root cause: several paths round-trip `int64` values through `float64`, which only has a 53-bit mantissa. This produces wrong answers well away from the bounds, not just at them.

### 2a. Scalar `Timedelta.__mul__` / `__truediv__`

Integral operands are applied in `float64`, so an exactly-representable result comes back wrong, or wrongly raises:

```python
Timedelta.min / 1      # AssertionError    <- should be Timedelta.min
Timedelta.max / 1      # OverflowError     <- should be Timedelta.max
Timedelta.min * 1.0    # AssertionError    <- should be Timedelta.min

# off-by-one above 2**53; numpy and Series/2 both give ...983
Timedelta(36028797018963967, "ns") / 2                          # 18014398509481984 ns
np.timedelta64(36028797018963967, "ns") / 2                     # 18014398509481983 ns
```

`__mul__` also never normalizes numpy integer scalars, so the product stays an `int64` multiply and **wraps silently** — while the Python-`int` and vectorized forms both raise:

```python
Timedelta(2**62, "ns") * np.int64(4)   # Timedelta('0 days')   <- silent wrap (RuntimeWarning only)
Timedelta(2**62, "ns") * 4             # OverflowError
pd.Series([Timedelta(2**62, "ns")]) * np.int64(4)
                                       # OutOfBoundsTimedelta: O

train.title: BUG: tz_localize misreports wall times whose UTC value is unrepresentable (NaT sentinel, int64 wrap, OOB read)
train.body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from dateutil.tz import gettz

# (1) Asia/Tokyo ran on LMT +09:18:59 in 1677, so this wall time's UTC value is
#     exactly iNaT.  It is unrepresentable, but nothing says so.
ts = pd.Timestamp("1677-09-21 09:31:42.145224192")

ts.tz_localize("Asia/Tokyo")
# ValueError: 1677-09-21 09:31:42.145224192 is a nonexistent time due to
# daylight savings time. Try using the 'nonexistent' argument.
#   ^ there is no DST gap here; the wall time exists, its UTC value does not

ts.tz_localize("Asia/Tokyo", nonexistent="NaT")
# NaT                                                    <- silently

ts.tz_localize("Asia/Tokyo", nonexistent="shift_forward")
# Timestamp('1677-09-21 10:00:00+091859', tz='Asia/Tokyo')   <- plausible, wrong

# (2) same thing at the top end, via the zoneinfo tz-rule fastpath
pd.Timestamp.max.tz_localize("US/Pacific")
# ValueError: 2262-04-11 23:47:16.854775807 is a nonexistent time due to
# daylight savings time.

# (3) the vectorised fixed-offset path does not check at all
pd.DatetimeIndex([pd.Timestamp(-(2**63) + 8 * 3600 * 10**9)]).tz_localize("Etc/GMT-8")
# DatetimeIndex(['NaT'], dtype='datetime64[ns, Etc/GMT-8]', freq=None)

pd.Series(np.array(["1677-09-21T08:12:43.145224192"], dtype="M8[ns]"),
          dtype="M8[ns, Etc/GMT-8]")
# 0   NaT
# dtype: datetime64[ns, Etc/GMT-8]

# (4) out-of-bounds read: a `nonexistent=` shift landing past the last cached
#     DST transition indexes `info.deltas` at `ntrans`.  Same call, same build:
dti = pd.DatetimeIndex(["2015-03-08 02:30"])
dti.tz_localize(gettz("America/Boise"), nonexistent=pd.Timedelta(days=11_000))
# DatetimeIndex(['257383-01-02 22:07:35.427585-07:00'], ...)
dti.tz_localize(gettz("America/Boise"), nonexistent=pd.Timedelta(days=11_000))
# DatetimeIndex(['2045-04-18 19:30:00-07:00'], ...)

# (5) the reverse direction is unchecked too, and stores the corrupt value
dti = pd.DatetimeIndex(
    np.array([pd.Timestamp.min._value], dtype="M8[ns]")
).tz_localize("UTC").tz_convert("US/Pacific")

dti.tz_localize(None)   # ['2262-04-11T15:54:18.854775809']  <- 585 years off
dti.floor("D").asi8     # [9223311600000000000]              <- stored
dti.year                # [2262]
```

### Issue Description

`NPY_NAT` is `INT64_MIN`, so it is both the `NaT` sentinel and a value that ordinary
datetime arithmetic can land on. In `pandas/_libs/tslibs/tzconversion.pyx` it is *also*
`_get_utc_bounds`' internal "no candidate found" marker, so a wall time whose true UTC
value is the sentinel is indistinguishable from one that does not exist in the zone.

This is the timezone-conversion counterpart of #66510, which covered the parsing and
construction side and was fixed by #66520. The shift-to-UTC side was not, and there are a
few adjacent problems in the same block:

**(1)–(2) The sentinel is reported as a nonexistent time.** `_get_utc_bounds` writes
`NPY_NAT` into `result_a`/`result_b` to mean "no candidate". When the real UTC value *is*
`NPY_NAT`, the caller reads that as a DST gap and takes the `nonexistent=` path — so
`"raise"` gives a wrong diagnosis, `"NaT"` silently swallows it, and the shift modes
return a wrong-but-plausible timestamp. There is a second instance in the
zoneinfo/`has_tz_rule` fastpath, which does a raw `val - delta` that can also wrap int64;
sweeping all zones shows both shapes.

**(3) The vectorised `use_fixed` and `use_tzlocal` loops have no check at all.** GH-65353
added `checked_sub` to the scalar `tz_localize_to_utc_single`, but the array loops still

train.title: BUG: remaining NaT-sentinel and out-of-bounds gaps in datetimelike arithmetic (GH-66510 follow-ups)
train.body:
Follow-ups found while fixing GH-66510 for the vectorized offset paths. Each is pre-existing on
`main` (verified at `082e7739`) and out of scope for that PR, but they are the same family of bug:
arithmetic on the raw int64 datetime64 values either lands on the `NaT` sentinel or leaves the
representable range without being reported as such.

Filing as one issue because (1) and (2) each need their two halves fixed together, and the whole
set shares a root cause. Happy to split if that's easier to triage.

### 1. Adding a timedelta can silently produce `NaT`

`NPY_NAT` is `INT64_MIN`, so a result that lands exactly there is indistinguishable from `NaT`
downstream. `add_overflowsafe` checks for int64 overflow but not for this, and the scalar
`_Timestamp.__add__` does not check either:

```python
>>> pd.Timestamp.min + pd.Timedelta(-1, "ns")
NaT
>>> pd.DatetimeIndex([pd.Timestamp.min]) + pd.Timedelta(-1, "ns")
DatetimeIndex(['NaT'], dtype='datetime64[ns]', freq=None)
>>> pd.TimedeltaIndex([pd.Timedelta.min]) - pd.Timedelta(1, "ns")
TimedeltaIndex(['NaT'], dtype='timedelta64[ns]', freq=None)
>>> pd.PeriodIndex([pd.Period(ordinal=-2**63 + 1, freq="D")]) - 1
PeriodIndex(['NaT'], dtype='period[D]')
```

All four should raise `OutOfBoundsDatetime` / `OutOfBoundsTimedelta`. Both the scalar and the
array side need to change together — fixing only one would replace this with a scalar/array
disagreement.

>>> pd.Timestamp.max + pd.DateOffset(months=1)

```

Relatedly, because the month shift is materialized before the timedelta component is applied, a
composed offset whose *final* result is representable is rejected on the array path:

```python

>>> pd.DatetimeIndex([pd.Timestamp.max]) + pd.DateOffset(months=1, days=-31)
OverflowError: Overflow occurred at .../np_datetime.c:512

never stored.

`n` is held in a C `int`, so a multiple of `2**32` silently becomes a no-op:

```python
>>> dr = pd.date_range("2000-01-03", periods=1, unit="s")
>>> dr + pd.offsets.SemiMonthEnd(2**32)
DatetimeIndex(['2000-01-15'], dtype='datetime64[s]', freq=None)   # == SemiMonthEnd(0)
>>> dr + pd.offsets.QuarterEnd(2**32)
DatetimeIndex(['2000-03-31'], dtype='datetime64[s]', freq=None)   # == QuarterEnd(0)
```

`BusinessDay` and `Week` had the same bug; widening those to `int64_t` is what the GH-66510
follow-up PR does, and the same treatment applies here.

### 4. `ccalendar` truncates years above `2**31`

`dayofweek(int y, int m, int d)`, `year_add_months` and `month_add_months` take the year as a C
`int`, but `npy_datetimestruct.year` is `int64_t`. Reachable only at second resolution, where the
representable range runs to year ~2.9e11:

```python
>>> big = pd.DatetimeIndex(np.array([np.iinfo(np.int64).max], dtype="M8[s]"))
>>> big[0]

>>> big + pd.DateOffset(months=1)
DatetimeIndex(['219250469-01-04 15:30:07'], dtype='datetime64[s]', freq=None)   # wrapped
>>> big[0].weekday()
OverflowError: value too large to convert to int
```

train.title: ENH: Add limit_distance parameter to Series/DataFrame.interpolate
train.body:
### Feature Type

- [x] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [x] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

I wish I could use pandas' interpolate method such that I could pass a parameter 'limit_distance' which will make it so that when two values differ by more than limit_distance, pandas will not interpolate.

I think this is similar to how the existing limit parameter works to prevent interpolation when there are too many NaNs in between, but instead of counting missing values, it prevents interpolation if the actual coordinate or time gap between two valid points is too big.

I encountered this issue while trying to work on ECG data and was instructed not to interpolate over long gaps, I realized that the most efficient way is not to interpolate conditionally, but rather to interpolate and then filter (remove unwanted interpolations); I think this is due to CPu and cache optimization but I am deviating from the main topic, I had to write code to do it and I thought that this could be cleaner to have this feature built in pandas.

Also, I think this may be related to issue #64588, which discusses limiting by consecutive NaN count, but this feature request specifically targets limiting by the actual numerical distance or time gap between anchor points rather than the number of missing cells.)

### Feature Description

I already implemented and tested this functionality locally. Here is the core helper method handling the vectorized gap logic:

```python
def _interp_limit_distance(
    indices: np.ndarray,
    invalid: npt.NDArray[np.bool_],
    limit_distance: float | int | str | Timedelta,
    unit: str | None = None,
) -> np.ndarray:
    """
    Return index positions of invalid values that should not be filled
    because the x-axis distance between the surrounding valid points
    exceeds limit_distance.
    """
    # Normalize and validate limit_distance
    if isinstance(limit_distance, (str, Timedelta)):
        from pandas.core.tools.timedeltas import to_timedelta

        td = to_timedelta(limit_distance)
        if unit is not None:
            # Cast to matching NumPy timedelta unit ('s', 'ms', 'us', 'ns') then to int64
            threshold = td.to_numpy().astype(f"m8[{unit}]").astype(np.int64)
        else:
            threshold = td.value
    else:
        threshold = limit_distance

    if threshold <= 0:
        raise ValueError("limit_distance must be greater than 0")

    # Identify valid and invalid positions
    valid_pos = np.flatnonzero(~invalid)
    invalid_pos = np.flatnonzero(invalid)

    # everything is valid if there are less than 2 valid points
    # or if there are no NaNs (impossible/no need to interpolate)
    if len(valid_pos) < 2 or len(invalid_pos) == 0:
        return np.array([], dtype=np.int64)

    # For every NaN position, find the valid index immediately next to it
    right_idx = np.searchsorted(valid_pos, invalid_pos, side="left")

    # Only inspect NaNs that sit between two valid points (not leading/trailing NaNs)
    inside_mask = (right_idx > 0) & (right_idx < len(valid_pos))
    if not inside_mask.any():
        return np.array([], dtype=np.int64)

    # Map each interior NaN to its own array index and the array indexes
    # of the valid anchor points immediately to its left and right
    invalid_inside = invalid_pos[inside_mask]
    right_valid_pos = valid_pos[right_idx[inside_mask]]
    left_valid_pos = valid_pos[right_idx[inside_mask] - 1]

    # Calculate the physical x-axis gap across each NaN
    gap_sizes = np.abs(indices[right_valid_pos] - indices[left_valid_pos])

    if gap_sizes.dtype.kind in "mM":
        gap_sizes = gap_sizes.view("i8")

    # Return only the NaN positions where the gap exceeds the threshold
    return invalid_inside[gap_sizes > threshold]

train.title: BUG: read_csv c engine collapses distinct fields sharing a NUL-terminated prefix with dtype=object or dtype='category'
train.body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the main branch of pandas.

### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd
from io import BytesIO

data = b'a\n"x\x00y"\n"x\x00z"\n"x"\n'

pd.read_csv(BytesIO(data), dtype=object, keep_default_na=False)["a"].tolist()
# c engine:      ['x\x00y', 'x\x00y', 'x\x00y']    <- all three rows became row 1
# python engine: ['x\x00y', 'x\x00z', 'x']

pd.read_csv(BytesIO(data), dtype="category", keep_default_na=False)["a"].tolist()
# c engine:      ['x', 'x', 'x']                   <- collapsed *and* truncated
# python engine: ['x\x00y', 'x\x00z', 'x']
```

### Issue Description

The `c` engine interns object-dtype field values in a hash table keyed on the NUL-terminated word (`kh_strbox_t`, via `kh_put_strbox`), so hashing and comparison stop at the first embedded NUL. Three fields that are distinct but share the prefix `x` before their first NUL all hash and compare equal, so rows 2 and 3 are silently boxed to the value from row 1. No error is raised; the data is simply wrong.

`dtype="category"` has the same defect in its own table (`_categorical_convert`), and additionally truncates the category labels themselves because they are boxed with `PyUnicode_FromString`.

Same root cause as GH-34551 (`unique` / `factorize` / `groupby` collapsing such values) and GH-19886 (`na_values` matching only up to a NUL): pandas keys several khash tables on a bare `const char *`, which hashes to the first NUL and compares with `strcmp`.

Filing for the record — this is fixed by GH-66512, which replaces those keys with an explicit (pointer, length) pair.

### Expected Behavior

Distinct fields should stay distinct, and category labels should not be truncated. Both should match `engine="python"`.

### Installed Versions

<details>

Reproduced on main at `7986b42596f` (3.1.0.dev0).

</details>

train.title: BUG: read_csv c engine silently truncates integer and boolean fields at an embedded NUL byte
train.body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.
- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the main branch of pandas.

### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd
from io import BytesIO

# integer converter stops at the NUL and accepts the truncated prefix
pd.read_csv(BytesIO(b'a\n1\n"1\x00xyz"\n3\n'))["a"].tolist()
# c engine:      [1, 1, 3]                       dtype int64
# python engine: ['1', '1\x00xyz', '3']          dtype str

# same for bool
pd.read_csv(BytesIO(b'a\nTrue\n"True\x00xyz"\nFalse\n'))["a"].tolist()
# c engine:      [True, True, False]             dtype bool
# python engine: ['True', 'True\x00xyz', 'False'] dtype str

# and for the nullable boolean path
pd.read_csv(BytesIO(b'a\n1\x00x\nTrue\n'), dtype="boolean")["a"].tolist()
# c engine:      [True, True]
# python engine: raises ValueError: 1\x00x cannot be cast to bool
```

### Issue Description

A field containing an embedded NUL byte is parsed only up to that NUL by the `c` engine's numeric and boolean converters, so `"1\x00xyz"` is accepted as the integer `1` and `"True\x00xyz"` as `True`. The trailing bytes are silently discarded and no error is raised, so a column of junk can be read as a clean numeric or boolean column.

`engine="python"` rejects these values, leaving the column as strings (or raising, for `dtype="boolean"`), so the two engines disagree.

The cause is that `str_to_int64` / `str_to_uint64` in `pandas/_libs/src/parser/tokenizer.c` finish on `*endptr` rather than checking that the parse consumed the whole token, `to_boolean` compares with `strcasecmp`, and `_bool_numeric_literal` in `pandas/_libs/parsers.pyx` makes the same NUL-terminated assumption. Each token's exact length is already available at all of these call sites via `_token_len`.

Note these are entangled and should be fixed together: `to_boolean` backs the default `bool` path while `_bool_numeric_literal` backs `dtype="boolean"`, so fixing only one leaves the two disagreeing with each other. In particular `_bool_numeric_literal` lives in `parsers.pyx`, not `tokenizer.c`, so a fix scoped to the C tokenizer alone would miss it.

**Not affected:** the float path. `"1.5\x00xyz"` reads as `1.5` on *both* engines, because `lib.maybe_convert_numeric` truncates the same way, so there is no divergence to fix there.

This is a sibling of GH-19886 and GH-34551 (same root cause: values handled as NUL-terminated C strings). It was deliberately left out of GH-66511 / GH-66512 / GH-66513 to keep those focused.

### Expected Behavior

`"1\x00xyz"` should not parse as an integer and `"True\x00xyz"` should not parse as `True`. The `c` engine should agree with `engine="python"`.

### Installed Versions

<details>

Reproduced on main at `7986b42596f` (3.1.0.dev0).

</details>

train.title: BUG: IntervalArray silently builds interval[int64] with an object-dtype right side
train.body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

arr = pd.arrays.IntervalArray([pd.Interval(0, 2**64)])

arr.dtype          # interval[int64, right]
arr.dtype.subtype  # int64
arr.left.dtype     # int64
arr.right.dtype    # object     <- contradicts the advertised subtype
arr.length.dtype   # object
arr.mid.dtype      # object

# the mirror image, with the oversized value on the left, is rejected
pd.arrays.IntervalArray([pd.Interval(-(2**64), 0)])
# TypeError: category, object, and string subtypes are not supported for IntervalArray
```

`pd.IntervalIndex([pd.Interval(0, 2**64)])` produces the same inconsistent state.

### Issue Description

When only the *right* endpoint falls outside the `int64` range, `IntervalArray` builds an array
whose declared dtype disagrees with its own data: `dtype` says `interval[int64, right]` while
`right.dtype` is `object`. Every derived quantity inherits the inconsistency (`length`, `mid`),
and `arr.astype(arr.dtype)` does not repair it.

`IntervalArray._ensure_simple_new_inputs` only ever consults `left.dtype`:

- the object/category/string rejection checks `left.dtype` alone
  ([interval.py:324](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/main/pandas/core/arrays/interval.py#L324)), so an object
  *right* side passes;
- the dtype is then derived from `left.dtype` alone
  ([interval.py:365](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/main/pandas/core/arrays/interval.py#L365));
- the signed/unsigned mismatch check
  ([interval.py:370-378](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/main/pandas/core/arrays/interval.py#L370-L378))
  requires *both* `left_dtype.kind` and `right_dtype.kind` to be in `"iu"`, so an `object` right
  side (kind `"O"`) skips that guard too.

The asymmetry is the clearest symptom: putting the oversized value on the left raises a clean
`TypeError`, while putting it on the right silently produces a corrupt array.

### Expected Behavior

Either outcome would be consistent; the current side-dependent behavior is not:

- raise the same `TypeError` regardless of which endpoint has the unsupported dtype, or
- derive the subtype from both endpoints so the resulting `dtype` actually describes the data.

At minimum `arr.dtype.subtype` should never disagree with `arr.left.dtype` / `arr.right.dtype`.

### Installed Versions

<details>

```

------------------

python                : 3.13.11
python-bits           : 64
OS                    : Darwin
OS-release            : 23.3.0
pandas                : 3.0.5
numpy                 : 2.5.1

train.title: BUG: convert_dtypes raises OverflowError for integers outside the int64 range
train.body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

pd.Series([2**64], dtype=object).convert_dtypes()
# OverflowError: Python int too large to convert to C long

pd.Series([-(2**63) - 1], dtype=object).convert_dtypes()
# OverflowError: Python int too large to convert to C long
```

### Issue Description

`Series` construction correctly infers `object` for an integer that no NumPy/nullable integer
dtype can hold:

```python
>>> pd.Series([2**64]).dtype
dtype('O')
```

but `convert_dtypes` then tries to force that column to `Int64` regardless, and overflows:

```
  File "pandas/core/internals/blocks.py", line 582, in convert_dtypes
    rbs.append(b.astype(dtype=dtype, squeeze=b.ndim != 1))
  File "pandas/core/dtypes/astype.py", line 82, in _astype_nansafe
    return dtype.construct_array_type()._from_sequence(arr, dtype=dtype, copy=copy)
  File "pandas/core/arrays/numeric.py", line 248, in _coerce_to_data_and_mask
    values = dtype_cls._safe_cast(values, dtype, copy=False)
  File "pandas/core/arrays/integer.py", line 65, in _safe_cast
    casted = values.astype(dtype, copy=copy)
OverflowError: Python int too large to convert to C long
```

`lib.infer_dtype` reports `"integer"` for these values, and the object-block conversion maps
that straight to `Int64` without checking that the values actually fit. `IntegerArray._safe_cast`
first attempts `astype(..., casting="safe")`, which raises `TypeError` for object input, and the
fallback `values.astype(dtype)` is what raises `OverflowError`.

Note this is a plain `OverflowError` escaping a public API rather than a pandas error type, so
it is also not catchable via anything in `pandas.errors`.

### Expected Behavior

`convert_dtypes` should leave the column as `object` when the values do not fit in the target
integer dtype, matching what construction already infers:

```python
>>> pd.Series([2**64], dtype=object).convert_dtypes().dtype
dtype('O')
```

Raising a clear pandas-level error would also be defensible, but silently attempting `Int64` and
surfacing a raw `OverflowError` is not.

train.title: BUG: Timestamp.replace(nanosecond=...) can produce a Timestamp whose value is the NaT sentinel
train.body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

ts = pd.Timestamp.min.replace(nanosecond=192)

ts
# Timestamp('1677-09-21 00:12:43.145224192')   <- looks like an ordinary Timestamp

ts._value
# -9223372036854775808                          <- but this is iNaT

ts is pd.NaT        # False
pd.isna(ts)         # False
ts == ts            # True

pd.Series([ts])
# 0   NaT
# dtype: datetime64[ns]
```

### Issue Description

`Timestamp.min` is `1677-09-21 00:12:43.145224193`, i.e. `iNaT + 1`. Replacing the
nanosecond field with `192` names the wall time one nanosecond earlier, whose int64
representation is exactly `iNaT` (`-2**63`).

`npy_datetimestruct_to_datetime` returns that value without raising, and `replace` does
not check for it, so we construct a `Timestamp` whose `_value` is the NaT sentinel but
which is not `NaT`. It reprs as a normal timestamp, `pd.isna` reports `False`, and it
compares equal to itself — the corruption only surfaces once the value reaches array-land,
where it is reinterpreted as `NaT`:

```python
pd.Series([ts]).iloc[0]          # NaT
pd.DatetimeIndex([ts])[0]        # NaT
```

It is a single-value hole. The neighbours behave correctly:

```python
pd.Timestamp.min.replace(nanosecond=191)
# OutOfBoundsDatetime: Out of bounds timestamp: 1677-09-21 00:12:43 with frequency 'ns'

pd.Timestamp.min.replace(nanosecond=193)
# Timestamp('1677-09-21 00:12:43.145224193')   (== Timestamp.min)
```

so only `nanosecond=192` slips through, because it is the one out-of-bounds value that
lands on the sentinel rather than past it.

The same class of hole exists in the `Timestamp` constructor's `nanosecond=` keyword
(`Timestamp(datetime(1677, 9, 21, 0, 12, 43, 145224), nanosecond=192)` returns `NaT`
instead of raising); I have a fix for the constructor side in progress and will reference
this issue from it.

### Expected Behavior

`Timestamp.min.replace(nanosecond=192)` should raise `OutOfBoundsDatetime`, like
`nanosecond=191` already does. A `Timestamp` should never hold `iNaT` as its `_value`
while reporting itself as non-null.

### Installed Versions

<details>

Reproduced on `main` at 644979a084f (3.1.0.dev0).

</details>

train.title: BUG: read_parquet(to_pandas_kwargs={"self_destruct": True}) segfaults
train.body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd, numpy as np

pd.DataFrame(np.random.rand(1000, 20)).to_parquet("/tmp/t.parquet")
pd.read_parquet("/tmp/t.parquet", to_pandas_kwargs={"self_destruct": True})
# SIGSEGV, exit 139, no traceback
```

### Issue Description

Passing self_destruct=True through to_pandas_kwargs segfaults the interpreter.

to_pandas_kwargs is 3.0 only. On 2.3.3 the argument falls through to pyarrow.parquet.read_table and raises TypeError, so this looks specific to the 3.0 passthrough.

I ran each case in its own subprocess:


| case | result |
|---|---|
| `{"self_destruct": True}` | Crashes (signal 11) |
| `{"self_destruct": True, "split_blocks": True}` | Crashes (signal 11) |
| `{"split_blocks": True}` | ok |
| `{}` | ok |
| no `to_pandas_kwargs` | ok |

So the trigger is self_destruct, and there is nothing wrong with the passthrough itself. I get the same results on macOS/arm64 and Linux/x86-64, both on pandas 3.0.5 with pyarrow 25.0.0.

The conversion is not where it crashes. If you do it in two steps, the fault is on the following access to the table.

`import pyarrow.parquet as pq
t = pq.read_table("/tmp/t.parquet")
df = t.to_pandas(self_destruct=True)
print(df.shape)            # (1000, 20), conversion is fine
print(t.schema.metadata)   # SIGSEGV`


Root Cause:

pyarrow actually nulls out the table's internal pointer when self_destruct is set (pyarrow/table.pxi):

```
if c_options.self_destruct:
    # Move the shared_ptr, table is now unsafe to use further
    c_table = move(table.sp_table)
    table.table = NULL
```

The docstring for self_destruct says the same thing, that it is experimental and that using the object after conversion will crash the process.

PyArrowImpl.read does use the object after conversion. It reads pa_table.schema.metadata to pick up 

```
PANDAS_ATTRS:

python
result = arrow_table_to_pandas(
    pa_table, dtype_backend=dtype_backend, to_pandas_kwargs=to_pandas_kwargs,
)

if pa_table.schema.metadata:                     # NULL deref
    if b"PANDAS_ATTRS" in pa_table.schema.metadata:
        ..
```

### Expected Behavior

No segfault. The call should either return the DataFrame:

    df = pd.read_parquet("/tmp/t.parquet", to_pandas_kwargs={"self_destruct": True})
    # DataFrame, 1000 x 20

or raise if `self_destruct` isn't supported through this path.

### Pandas version checks

### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame([[1, 2]], columns=["A", "B"])

headers = pd.Series(["X", "Y"], name=4)

df = df.set_axis(headers, axis="columns")

print(df.columns)
print(df.columns.name)

df.query("X == 1")
```

### Issue Description

DataFrame.query() raises an IndexError when the column Index has a numeric name.

After assigning column labels using DataFrame.set_axis() with a Series, the resulting column Index inherits the Series.name. If this name is an integer, DataFrame.query() fails, even though the columns are a regular one-dimensional Index rather than a MultiIndex.

This appears to be caused by query() (or one of its internal helpers) interpreting the numeric Index.name as a level number instead of as the name of the index.

The issue disappears if the column index name is removed:

```python
df.columns.name = None
```

or

```python
headers = headers.rename(None)
```

This suggests that the failure is specifically related to an integer-valued `Index.name`.

### Expected Behavior

DataFrame.query() should work regardless of the value or type of df.columns.name.

The following should execute successfully:

headers = pd.Series(["X", "Y"], name=4)

df = df.set_axis(headers, axis="columns")

df.query("X == 1")

without raising an exception.

Alternatively, if integer-valued axis names are not supported, this should be documented or rejected earlier with a more informative error message.

train.title: DOC: Installation guide uses outdated "source activate" conda syntax
train.body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that the issue still exists on the latest versions of the docs on `main` [here](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/)

### Location of the documentation

https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/getting_started/install.html#installing-with-conda

### Documentation problem

The Installation guide instructs users to activate a conda environment using legacy syntax:
```
# On Linux or MacOS
source activate name_of_my_env
# On Windows
activate name_of_my_env
```
`source activate` / `activate` was conda's activation syntax before conda 4.4 (released in 2017), and has since been replaced by `conda activate` which works across all operating systems (e.g. Windows, MacOS, Linux). 

Moreover, the "[Creating a development environment](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/development/contributing_environment.html#option-1-using-conda-recommended)" guide in the pandas documentation already uses `conda activate pandas-dev` as its primary instruction. This makes the two pandas documentation pages inconsistent with each other, and with current conda usage as well.

### Suggested fix for documentation

Replace the  `source activate` / `activate` instructions with the single modern command:
```
conda activate name_of_my_env
```
I'd like to work on this myself and will submit a PR with the fix.

train.title: BUG: unexercised divmod/rdivmod in tests / always False assertion
train.body:
Hello. Wasn't really using `pandas` - I was testing something inside `ruff`, but I've stumbled upon the following test in pandas codebase:

https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/3ea5174d8f7280be22a41b7f4d45ed32db9bc07b/pandas/tests/scalar/test_na_scalar.py#L65-L66

Note that it's using `op(NA, other) is (NA, NA)` - `(NA, NA)` will result in a fresh tuple object on each run, so there's no way `op(NA, other)` had the same object, so effectively this assertion is always false. 

I don't fully understand the semantics of the test, but the typical fix for this to use `==` -  `op(NA, other) == (NA, NA)`, instead of relying on `is`.

Generic Python example:	
```python
>>> a = object()
>>> (a, a) is (a, a)
False
>>> (a, a) is (a, a)
False
>>> (a, a) is (a, a)
False
>>> (a, a) == (a, a)
True
>>> (a, a) == (a, a)
True
>>> (a, a) == (a, a)
True
```

Example with pandas:
```python
>>> from pandas._libs.missing import NA
>>> result = divmod(NA, 3)
>>> result
(<NA>, <NA>)
>>> result is (NA, NA)
False
>>> result == (NA, NA)
True
```

But in theory CI should have flagged it, if it would be just always-false assertion and the code above was introduced a while ago - https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/commit/48368ad6f9087e2e4e4c5236d5492a412ce9d826, so there's another part to this story.

This test is using `all_arithmetic_functions` fixture:
https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/3ea5174d8f7280be22a41b7f4d45ed32db9bc07b/pandas/conftest.py#L1097-L1115

Looking at the list of params, divmod / rdivmod doesn't seem to be ever exercised, therefore this error never surfaced.
So this branch is a dead code and to avoid slipping errors needs a coverage that can be provided by adding `divmod` and `rdivmo` to the fixture parameters.

train.title: BUG: ujson_dumps can segfault when Python API return values are not checked during encoding
train.body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import decimal

import pandas._libs._ujson as ujson


# Very large integer used as a dictionary key
ujson.ujson_dumps({1 << 1_000_000: "value"})


# Decimal subclass returning an invalid Unicode surrogate
LONE_SURROGATE = "\ud800"


class InvalidDecimal(decimal.Decimal):
    def __format__(self, *args, **kwargs):
        return LONE_SURROGATE


ujson.ujson_dumps(InvalidDecimal(1))
```

### Issue Description

There are several Python C API call patterns in `ujson`'s `objToJSON` implementation where the return value or error state is not reliably checked.

Failures can occur while:

* converting Unicode values to UTF-8, for example when processing `"\ud800"`
* converting extremely large integers to strings
* calling special methods that normally return predictable values but may be overridden by subclasses

Instead of propagating a Python exception, some of these cases can cause a segmentation fault.

The issue was initially discovered through fuzz testing with the following input:

```python
ujson.ujson_dumps({1 << 1_000_000: "value"})
```

A broader review of `objToJSON` identified several additional inputs that may trigger crashes.

## Known Crash Cases

The following unusual or malformed inputs may cause `ujson_dumps` to segfault:

* `decimal.Decimal` subclasses whose `__format__` method returns a lone surrogate
* `datetime.time` subclasses whose `isoformat()` method returns:

  * a non-string value
  * a string containing a lone surrogate
* objects whose `__dir__` method raises an exception
* objects whose `__dir__` result contains a lone surrogate
* `set` subclasses whose `__iter__` method raises an exception
* integer values whose string representation exceeds `sys.get_int_max_str_digits()`
* dictionary keys containing lone surrogate values
* dictionary keys containing integers that are too large to convert to strings
* dictionary keys whose `__str__` method returns a lone surrogate
* `labels` arrays containing invalid surrogate values

Related fixes may overlap with:

* #66356
* #66357

Most of these inputs are unusual and cannot normally be produced by simply processing untrusted JSON-compatible data. The very large integer case is the most straightforward exception.


### Expected Behavior

`ujson_dumps` should never crash or segfault.

When an internal Python API call fails, the encoder should:

1. detect the failure
2. stop encoding safely
3. propagate an appropriate Python exception

### Installed Versions

Please add the output of:

```python
import pandas as pd

pd.show_versions()
```

train.title: BUG: read_sas segfaults on a SAS7BDAT file with an out-of-range row_length in the header
train.body:
### Pandas version checks

- [X] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.
- [X] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.
- [X] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.

### Reproducible Example

`read_sas` segfaults on a SAS7BDAT file whose header declares a large `row_length`. No corruption of the *data* is needed — four bytes of metadata are enough.

```python
import struct
import pandas as pd

# pandas' own test file; the row_length field lives in the row-size subheader
src = "pandas/tests/io/sas/data/test1.sas7bdat"
data = bytearray(open(src, "rb").read())
assert struct.unpack("<I", data[130612:130616])[0] == 816  # row_length
data[130612:130616] = struct.pack("<I", 0x7FFFFFF0)
open("crash.sas7bdat", "wb").write(bytes(data))

pd.read_sas("crash.sas7bdat")   # Segmentation fault: 11
```

```
$ python -X faulthandler repro.py
Fatal Python error: Segmentation fault

Current thread 0x00000001d8f81c40 (most recent call first):
  File "pandas/io/sas/sas7bdat.py", line 736 in read
  File "pandas/io/sas/sasreader.py", line 214 in read_sas
$ echo $?
139
```

Crash report frames:

```
sas.cpython-313-darwin.so  __pyx_f_6pandas_5_libs_3sas_6Parser_process_byte_array_with_data
sas.cpython-313-darwin.so  __pyx_f_6pandas_5_libs_3sas_6Parser_readline
sas.cpython-313-darwin.so  __pyx_pw_6pandas_5_libs_3sas_6Parser_9read
EXC_BAD_ACCESS (SIGSEGV), KERN_INVALID_ADDRESS
```

### Issue Description

`Parser.process_byte_array_with_data` takes its bounds as C `int`:

https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/main/pandas/_libs/sas.pyx#L541

```cython
cdef void process_byte_array_with_data(self, int offset, int length) except *:
    ...
    assert offset + length <= self.cached_page_len, "Out of bounds read"
    source = Buffer(&self.cached_page[offset], length)
```

`length` is `row_length`, read straight from the file as an unsigned int. When it is near `INT_MAX`, `offset + length` overflows signed `int` and wraps negative, so the guard passes. `Buffer` is then constructed with a ~2GB `length` over a 64KB page. `buf_get`'s own `assert offset < buf.length` is satisfied for reads far past the real allocation, so every subsequent read is unchecked and the process dies on a wild address.

A more modest `row_length` (e.g. `0x20000000`) is caught cleanly by the assert — it is specifically the overflow that defeats it. Widening these parameters to `int64_t`/`Py_ssize_t` and validating `row_length` against the page size after parsing the row-size subheader would fix it.

This is **not** fixed by #66469, which validates
`offsets[j] + lengths[j] <= row_length` once in `Parser.__init__`. That check passes
trivially here — the column offsets and lengths are untouched, it is `row_length` itself
that is out of range — so the crash above reproduces with #66469 applied.

Two related unchecked accesses in the same loop, noted for completeness:

1. The 8-byte fast path added in #65363 reads without a bounds check, unlike the `else`
   branch it replaced, which used the checked `buf_get`. **Already fixed by #66469**;
   mentioned here only because it shares this function and I hit it while narrowing down
   the crash.

2. The function is `@cython.boundscheck(False)` / `@cython.wraparound(False)`, and the
   destination index `m = s + 8 - lngt` goes negative for a decimal column declaring
   `lngt > 8`. Nothing validates `3 <= lngt <= 8`, and #66469's check does not catch it
   either (a column can declare `lngt > 8` while still fitting inside the row). Patching
   column 0 of `test1.sas7bdat` to declare length 16 does not crash, but writes 8 bytes
   in front of `byte_chunk` and returns a silently wrong frame.

`row_count`, `column_count`, and the subheader offset/length pairs are also file-controlled
and reach this arithmetic; a too-

- [X] Changing existing functionality in pandas

### Problem Description

`read_sas` defaults to `encoding=None`, which returns character columns as object-dtype `bytes`:

```python
>>> pd.read_sas("test1.sas7bdat")["Column2"]
0    b'pear'
dtype: object
```

sas7bdat files record their encoding in the header, so pandas can usually decode without being told. It is also now the only pandas reader that returns bytes by default.

### Feature Description

Deprecate the current default and change it to `encoding="infer"`, which decodes using the header-declared encoding (falling back to `latin-1` when the code is unrecognized). For XPORT, which has no encoding field, `"infer"` means `ISO-8859-1` — matching `XportReader`'s own default, which `read_sas` currently overrides with `None`.

`encoding=None` stays available for users who want raw bytes.

### Alternative Solutions

Leave the default and require every user to pass `encoding=`.

train.title: BUG: Series.dt.to_pydatetime() returns a Series with a reset RangeIndex instead of preserving the parent index
train.body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series(pd.to_datetime(["2026-01-01", "2026-02-01", "2026-03-01"]), index=[10, 11, 12])

print(s.dt.to_pydatetime().index)  # RangeIndex(start=0, stop=3, step=1)
print(s.dt.date.index)             # Index([10, 11, 12], dtype='int64')
print(s.dt.normalize().index)      # Index([10, 11, 12], dtype='int64')

 practical consequence is silent misalignment whenever the result is combined
with anything carrying the original index — for example a `groupby` slice, whose
index does not start at zero for any group after the first:

import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "g": ["a", "a", "b", "b"],
    "ts": pd.to_datetime(["2026-01-01", "2026-01-02", "2026-01-03", "2026-01-04"]),
    "x": [1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0],
})

for key, sub in df.groupby("g"):
    out = pd.DataFrame({"ts": sub["ts"].dt.to_pydatetime(), "x": sub["x"]})
    print(key, len(sub), "->", len(out))


Output:


a 2 -> 2
b 2 -> 4


Group `b` is silently doubled and half-NaN:


                    ts    x
0  2026-01-03 00:00:00  NaN
1  2026-01-04 00:00:00  NaN
2                  NaN  3.0
3                  NaN  4.0
```

### Issue Description

`Series.dt.to_pydatetime()` changed from returning an `ndarray` (pandas 2.x) to
returning a `Series` (pandas 3.0). That return-type change was deprecated ahead
of time and is not what this report is about.

The problem is that the new `Series` is built without the parent index:

https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/main/pandas/core/indexes/accessors.py

```python
def to_pydatetime(self) -> Series:
    # GH#20306
    from pandas import Series

    return Series(self._get_values().to_pydatetime(), dtype=object)
```

There is no `index=self._parent.index`, so the result always comes back on a
fresh `RangeIndex`. Every other `.dt` accessor result preserves the index, which
makes this an inconsistency rather than a deliberate choice as far as I can tell.

It fails silently: no exception and no warning. Code that used to get an
index-free `ndarray` under 2.x, and therefore aligned positionally, now aligns on
a `RangeIndex` that happens to be wrong. Where the original index is contiguous
from 0 the results still agree, so the breakage is invisible in the common case
and appears only on reindexed or grouped data.

Two smaller points in the same area:

1. The docstring's `Returns` section still reads `numpy.ndarray` /
   "Object dtype array containing native Python datetime objects", which no
   longer matches the annotated `-> Series` return type.
2. `ArrowTemporalProperties.to_pydatetime()` takes a different path
   (`ArrowExtensionArray._dt_to_pydatetime()`), so it is worth confirming the two
   accessors agree on index handling once this is fixed.

### Expected Behavior

`s.dt.to_pydatetime()` should return a `Series` carrying `s`'s index, consistent
with `s.dt.date`, `s.dt.normalize()`, and the other `.dt` accessors:

```
Series(self._get_values().to_pydatetime(), index=self._parent.index, dtype=object)
```

```

------------------

python-bits           : 64
OS                    : Windows
OS-release            : 11
Version               : 10.0.26200

train.title: ENH: UnicodeDecodeError from read_csv could suggest common alternative encodings
train.body:
### Feature Type

- [ ] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [x] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

I wish read_csv's UnicodeDecodeError gave me a hint about what to try next, instead of just failing with no direction.

When read_csv hits a UnicodeDecodeError (e.g. a Windows Excel export saved as cp1252), the error gives no indication that trying a different encoding is the likely fix.

Reproducible example (pandas 3.0.2):

with open('test.csv', 'wb') as f:
    f.write(b'name,note\n')
    f.write(b'test,em' + bytes([0x97]) + b'dash\n')  # valid cp1252, invalid utf-8

import pandas as pd
pd.read_csv('test.csv')

Result:
UnicodeDecodeError: 'utf-8' codec can't decode byte 0x97 in position 17: invalid start byte

This is a very common situation, Windows Excel commonly exports CSVs as cp1252, not utf-8, and the fix is almost always trying encoding='latin-1' or encoding='cp1252'. But nothing in the error message points there, so new users often don't realize encoding is even the problem.

### Feature Description

Append a short hint to the UnicodeDecodeError raised during CSV parsing when the default utf-8 encoding fails and the user hasn't explicitly set encoding.

Rough approach, in the CSV reading error handling path:

try:
    ...read with utf-8...
except UnicodeDecodeError as e:
    if encoding_was_default:
        raise UnicodeDecodeError(
            e.encoding, e.object, e.start, e.end,
            e.reason + ". Tip: this file may not be UTF-8 encoded. "
            "Try encoding='latin-1' or encoding='cp1252', common with Windows Excel exports."
        ) from e
    raise

This only changes the message text, not behavior, and only fires when encoding wasn't explicitly passed by the user, so it doesn't affect anyone who already specifies an encoding.

### Alternative Solutions

Currently the only options are:

1. Manually try common encodings one by one (utf-8, latin-1, cp1252) until one works, usually after searching Stack Overflow to learn this is the fix
2. Use a third-party library like chardet or charset-normalizer to detect the encoding beforehand, which is a heavier dependency for a one-line hint
3. Open the file in a text editor that reports encoding, then pass it explicitly

None of these are discoverable from the error message itself, which is the actual gap this request addresses.

### Additional Context

This is intentionally scoped narrower than a full encoding='detect' feature, since I understand that's a bigger design discussion. This is just improving the existing error message text for the common case.

train.title: BUG: Segfaults from various python api call return values not being checked during encode by ujson
train.body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas._libs._ujson as ujson
ujson.ujson_dumps({1 << 1_000_000: "value"})

LONE_SURROGATE = "\ud800"

class InvalidDecimal(decimal.Decimal):
    def __format__(self, *a, **kw):
        return LONE_SURROGATE
ujson.ujson_dumps(InvalidDecimal(1))
```

### Issue Description

There are three python api call patterns that ujson objToJson doesn't reliably check the result code for:
 - Converting unicode to utf8. (for example "\ud800" can fail)
 - Converting very large integers to string
 - Calling Various dunder methods that usually behave predicably.

I came into this via some fuzz testing I was doing, which found this:

```
ujson.ujson_dumps({1 << 1_000_000: "value"})
```

But then a review of the `objToJSON` with the help of codex came up with the following inputs that cause ujson to segfault:
 - [X] decimal.Decimal subclasses with a `__format__` method that returns a lone surrogate [#66357]
 - [X] `datetime.time` subclasses whose `isoformat()` return a non-string, or lone surrogate value [#66357]
 - [ ] `__dir__` methods on objects that raise
 - [ ] `__dir__` methods on objects that return a lone surrogate value.
 - [ ] Set() subclasses whose `__iter__` raises
 - [X] encoding int values whose string representation > `sys.get_int_max_str_digits()` digits long [#66357]
 - [ ] `dict` keys that are lone surrogate values
 - [ ] `dict` keys that are `int` values that are too long
 - [ ] `dict` keys that are are objects whose `__str__()` method returns a lone surrogate.
 - [ ] 'labels' arrays with invalid surrogate values

All of these are unusual/obscure cases, and apart from the massive int case, are not exercisable just by processing 'untrusted' data.

The fixes here are just to check the respective python api calls and handle them appropriately.

<details>
<summary>Unit tests</summary>

```
LONE_SURROGATE = "\ud800"

def test_encode_invalid_decimal_subclass(self):
    class InvalidDecimal(decimal.Decimal):
        def __format__(self, *a, **kw):
            return LONE_SURROGATE

    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="surrogates not allowed"):
        ujson.ujson_dumps(InvalidDecimal(1))

def test_encode_dict_with_lone_surrogate_key(self):
    lone_surrogate_dict = {LONE_SURROGATE: "value1"}
    with pytest.raises(UnicodeEncodeError, match="surrogates not allowed"):
        ujson.ujson_dumps(lone_surrogate_dict)

def test_encode_time_invalid_subclass_surrogate(self):
    class InvalidTime(datetime.time):
        def isoformat(self):
            return LONE_SURROGATE

    with pytest.raises(UnicodeEncodeError, match="surrogates not allowed"):
        ujson.ujson_dumps(InvalidTime())

def test_encode_time_invalid_subclass_non_str(self):
    class InvalidTime(datetime.time):
        def isoformat(self):
            return 1

    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="Failed to convert time"):
        ujson.ujson_dumps(InvalidTime())

def test_encode_object_bad_dir(self):
    class _TestObj:

train.title: DOC: Series.eq() fill_value docs outdated for string dtype
train.body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that the issue still exists on the latest versions of the docs on `main` [here](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/)


### Location of the documentation

https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.Series.eq


## Problem

The docs for `Series.eq()` specify that `fill_value` accepts `float | None` only.
However, passing a string `fill_value` works correctly at runtime when the Series has `dtype='string'`.

## Reproducible Example

import pandas as pd

s1 = pd.Series(["a", "b", None], dtype="string")
s2 = pd.Series(["a", "c", "d"], dtype="string")

result = s1.eq(s2, fill_value="missing")
print(result)

## Output
0     True
1    False
2    False
dtype: boolean

## Expected behavior

Docs should reflect that `fill_value` accepts a string value when 
dtype is `'string'`.

## Note

Originally raised by @geoffrey-eisenbarth in pandas-stubs#1797.

### Suggested fix for documentation

Update the `fill_value` parameter description in `Series.eq()` docs from:

> fill_value : float or None, default None

To:

> fill_value : float, str, or None, default None

train.title: REF: Reduce cognitive complexity of `tokenize_bytes`
train.body:
The [`tokenize_bytes`](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/15b1dd913e3df72854955936b0d89c7f95648a9a/pandas/_libs/src/parser/tokenizer.c#L779-L1357) function currently has a cognitive complexity score of 551 according to `clang-tidy`, which significantly exceeds the default threshold of 25.

The complexity primarily comes from managing 16 distinct parser states within a single monolithic loop, combined with inline SIMD preprocessing and scalar fallback logic. Modularizing the state handling into smaller helper functions would help improve the readability and long-term maintainability of the CSV parser.

train.title: BUG: False ChainedAssignmentError, misattributed to the caller, when setitem runs in Cython-compiled code — and no supported way to disable the check
train.body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example


Two files. `repro_mod.py` contains only a plain, legal column assignment on
a function-local DataFrame — no mask, no intermediate object, no second
subscript:

```python
# repro_mod.py
import pandas as pd


def legal_assignment():
    df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3]})
    df["b"] = df["a"] * 2
    return df

```
```python
# run_repro.py
import warnings

import pandas as pd

import repro_mod

with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught:
    warnings.simplefilter("always")
    df = repro_mod.legal_assignment()

assert df["b"].tolist() == [2, 4, 6]  # the assignment itself worked fine

chained = [w for w in caught
           if issubclass(w.category, pd.errors.ChainedAssignmentError)]

if not chained:
    print("OK: no warning")
else:
    for w in chained:
        print(f"FALSE POSITIVE: {w.category.__name__} "
              f"attributed to {w.filename}:{w.lineno}")
```

Run it twice — once with the module as plain Python, once after compiling
that same module into a C extension with Cython:

```shell
$ python run_repro.py
```
OK: no warning

```shell
$ cythonize -3 -i repro_mod.py
$ python run_repro.py
```
FALSE POSITIVE: ChainedAssignmentError attributed to ...\run_repro.py:10


Identical source, identical runner. Note the attribution: `run_repro.py:10`
is `df = repro_mod.legal_assignment()` — the *caller*, which performs no
assignment at all. In a larger application this misattribution points at
whatever pure-Python frame happens to sit below the compiled code (in ours,
the application's `MainLoop()` call in the entry module), which makes the
warning extremely hard to trace back to its real origin.

### Issue Description

`DataFrame.__setitem__` (pandas 3.0.3, `pandas/core/frame.py:4642`; the same
pattern guards every `ChainedAssignmentError` site in `frame.py`,
`series.py`, `generic.py`, and `indexing.py`) detects chained assignment
with two heuristics:

```python
if not CHAINED_WARNING_DISABLED:
    if sys.getrefcount(self) <= REF_COUNT and not com.is_local_in_caller_frame(self):
        warnings.warn(_chained_assignment_msg, ChainedAssignmentError, stacklevel=2)
```

Both heuristics assume the caller is interpreted CPython code, and both
misfire when the caller is a compiled extension:

1. **Refcount** — a Cython function keeps `df` in a C variable rather than
   in a frame's locals, so `sys.getrefcount(df)` inside `__setitem__` sits
   at the temporary-object level even though `df` is a genuine local.
2. **Frame inspection** — `is_local_in_caller_frame`
   (`pandas/core/common.py:662`) looks for the object in
   `sys._getframe(2).f_locals`. Cython functions do not create Python frame
   objects, so `sys._getframe(2)` skips past the real caller entirely and
   lands on an unrelated pure-Python frame further down the stack. The
   rescue check fails, and `stacklevel=2` attributes the warning to that
   unrelated frame.

The same failure mode applies to any frame-less caller (Cython, mypyc, and
similar ahead-of-time compilers).

Filtering the warning is not a real workaround: with
`warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=ChainedAssignmentError)` the
message disappears but the detection machinery still runs. Because the
refcount test always passes for compiled callers, **every** setitem from
compiled code takes the slow path — `sys._getframe(2)`, a full `f_locals`
materialisation, and the `warnings` machinery. We measured roughly 4 µs per
assignment on small frames (Python 3.11, Windows) — a permanent tax on
exactly the code that was compiled for speed.

A short-circuit for this already ex
