train.title: DOC: `to_numeric` "Returns" is missing Index and scalars, may have other problems
train.body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that the issue still exists on the latest versions of the docs on `main` [here](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/)


### Location of the documentation

https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/reference/api/pandas.to_numeric.html

> **Returns:**
> **ret**
> Numeric if parsing succeeded. Return type depends on input. Series if Series, otherwise ndarray.

### Documentation problem

The documentation is missing these return types:

### Index

1-d specifically

Example:
```py
>>> pd.to_numeric(pd.Index(['0']))
Index([0], dtype='int64')
```

Source:
https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/be0642f7cb8900282a43b53cd50cf00a05161ed6/pandas/core/tools/numeric.py#L318-L323

### Scalars

Example:
```py
>>> pd.to_numeric('0')
np.int64(0)
```

Source:
https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/be0642f7cb8900282a43b53cd50cf00a05161ed6/pandas/core/tools/numeric.py#L202-L210

https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/be0642f7cb8900282a43b53cd50cf00a05161ed6/pandas/core/tools/numeric.py#L324-L325

### Additionally

"Numeric if parsing succeeded" implies there's a different return type if parsing failed, but the function would actually **raise** in that case (instead of returning), if I understand correctly. Or it would return NaN, but that's still a numeric type, even though it's called "not a number".

Also, the `dtype_backend` parameter says: "Back-end data type applied to the resultant **DataFrame**", but `to_numeric` can't return a DataFrame as far as I know. I tried it just to confirm:
```py
>>> pd.to_numeric(pd.DataFrame([0]))
TypeError: arg must be a list, tuple, 1-d array, or Series

>>> pd.to_numeric(pd.DataFrame([0]), dtype_backend='pyarrow')
TypeError: arg must be a list, tuple, 1-d array, or Series

>>> pd.to_numeric(pd.DataFrame([0]), dtype_backend='numpy_nullable')
TypeError: arg must be a list, tuple, 1-d array, or Series
```

### Suggested fix for documentation

I don't understand all the ins and outs of the function, but I'll try my best:

Change "Returns" to:
> **Returns:**
> **numeric**
> Return type depends on input. For numeric inputs, the type is preserved. For scalars: `int` if possible, otherwise `float`. For 1-d: Series if Series, Index if Index, otherwise ndarray.

Change `dtype_backend` paramter to: "Back-end data type applied to the resultant Series or Index"

### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

data = [1, 2, 3, None, None, 6, 7]

r_nullable = s_arrow.interpolate(method="linear", limit_direction="forward")

```

### Issue Description

When interpolating a Series backed by a pyarrow dtype such as int64[pyarrow], `method="linear"` with `limit_direction="forward"` leaves missing values unchanged, while the equivalent series with a numpy backend interpolates as expected. The same pyarrow-backed series also appears to work with `limit_direction="backward"`.

### Expected Behavior

The pyarrow-backed series should interpolate consistently with the numpy backend, expected result is a of the form `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]`.

The expected behavior can be achieved in three ways:
1. Running the same code with pandas 2.3.3
2. Using `limit_direction=backward`:
```python
import pandas as pd

data = [1, 2, 3, None, None, 6, 7]
s_arrow = pd.Series(pd.array(data, dtype="int64[pyarrow]"))
r_backwards = s_arrow.interpolate(method="linear", limit_direction="backward")
print(r_backwards.to_list())
```
3. Using a numpy data type instead of the pyarrow type:
```python
import pandas as pd

data = [1, 2, 3, None, None, 6, 7]
s= pd.Series(pd.array(data, dtype="Int64"))
p= s.interpolate(method="linear", limit_direction="forward")

train.title: ENH: `df.duplicated()` default behavior should default to tagging all duplicates as `True`
train.body:
### Feature Type

- [ ] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [x] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

Hi, folks. I don't complain much about excellent open-source freeware, and I'm reasonably proficient at Pandas. I have about three years of solid use under my belt; before that, I had about six using Stata and am (was) a Stata maven. Pandas is generally much better...BUT...

`df.duplicated()` has what seems to me to be very confusing default behavior. In Stata, for example, one might use the equivalent duplicate-tagger function (in Stata, a "command") to locate people who are duplicates on a particular column to then hand inspect some of the rows to see if these are data entry errors or if, by contrast, one has perhaps missed a nuance and should expect a small number of duplicates on some col. This might sound sloppy, but when the codebook/docs for the DF sucks, this is a good way to figure out precisely what it might mean for a row to be a duplicate on some subset.

For that reason, I propose that `df.duplicated(keep=False)` should be the default behavior. I just spent around 30 minutes trying to figure out the problem with my code or possibly with the df, etc. because I was trying to locate people who are duplicates on a col that should in theory have a few duplicates but not many, and I could not actually see any duplicates after the following.

```
df["dupe"] = df.duplicated(subset=["year", "id"])
df.groupby("year").apply(lambda g :
    g["df"].mean())
df.loc[df["dupe"]==True].apply(foo)
```

Of course, I realized that this is because the default behavior is to *not* tag the first duplicate as a duplicate; in my case, since the multiplicity of a duplicate is almost always two, that meant that subsetting the data to only include duplicates was actually omitting those duplicates from view.

I did even skim the Docs, obviously inefficiently at first, but the wording *itself* seems extremely confusing. I did not realize that `keep=False` would solve my problems because this is not really about keep/drop behavior but tagging behavior. Changing the option's actual name to `tag` or something similar would probably lead to less confusion/make it more obvious that the default behavior is odd. 

On that note, another reason to change this, I think, is that there is no particular reason to expect the first duplicate to be the one to keep (at least without more context on the df; certainly, this is not true in general). This might make sense if it is a duplicate on all cols, but if the subset is anything but the full set of cols, this seems like behavior that might lead to very unexpected results. If someone does simply have outright duplicate records, it doesn't really cost significant time or memory (AFAICT) to then go back and set `keep="first"` once it's been confirmed that one might as well keep any record.

### Feature Description

I'm not a backend dev., merely a fairly tech-savvy sociologist. I think the technical side of this would be very easy.

### Alternative Solutions

People could read the docs very carefully before seeking other solutions.

### Additional Context

_No response_

train.body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame(
      {"val": [1, 2, 3]},
      index=pd.Index(pd.array([1, 2, 3], dtype="Int64"), name="id"),
  )
print(df.index.dtype)
print(df.rename({1: 9}).index.dtype)
```

### Issue Description

`DataFrame.rename()` and `Series.rename()` do not preserve nullable extension dtypes on index/column labels. In the reproduced cases with nullable integer and floating dtypes, renaming labels silently downcasts the result to the corresponding NumPy dtype.

The root cause appears to be `Index._transform_index()`, which reconstructs the transformed index from a plain Python list instead of preserving/casting through the original `ExtensionArray` dtype.

`rename()` should preserve the original index dtype after relabeling.

train.title: ENH: pd.crosstab with normalize='index' and margins=True drops the marginal 'Total' column.
train.body:
### Feature Type

- [ ] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [x] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

When creating a contingency table using pd.crosstab, if a user specifies normalize='index' while also requesting margins=True, the resulting DataFrame includes the marginal row (at the bottom) but excludes the marginal column (on the right). While the marginal column would mathematically consist of constants (1.0), its omission prevents the generation of a complete "framed" table for reporting and visualization purposes.

It is normal in data science to display both row and column totals in a crosstab.  If you select row or column as the sum, it's expect to show 100% on the non-selected column,  this is supported by the grand total selection where only the total in the bottom right is 100%.  This helps users quick understand what you are trying to convey and reinforces the choice of display 

The default should be to hide the result which is 1.0

### Feature Description

def _add_margins(self, table, margins_name):
    # CURRENT BEHAVIOR: 
    # Pandas calculates the sum of columns and rows.
    # If normalize='index', the row sum is always 1.0.
    
    # PROPOSED FIX:
    # Explicitly check if normalize is 'index' or 'columns' 
    # to prevent the 'Total' column/row from being optimized away.

    if self.normalize == 'index':
        # Force add the marginal column of 1.0s
        table[margins_name] = 1.0 
        
        # Calculate the marginal row (the distribution of the columns)
        # This is the mean of the normalized rows or a separate total calculation
        column_totals = table.iloc[:, :-1].mean(axis=0) 
        table.loc[margins_name] = column_totals
        table.at[margins_name, margins_name] = 1.0
        
    return table

### Alternative Solutions

none

train.title: API: Index.take discards fill_value and raises unnecessarily
train.body:
`Index.take` has two bugs when `allow_fill=True` and `fill_value` is passed explicitly:

### 1. `fill_value` is silently discarded

The caller's `fill_value` is ignored; `self._na_value` is always substituted:

```python
# Note: we discard fill_value and use self._na_value, only relevant
#  in the case where allow_fill is True and fill_value is not None
taken = algos.take(
    values, indices, allow_fill=allow_fill, fill_value=self._na_value
)
```

### 2. `_can_hold_na` gate raises on integer dtypes

```python
>>> pd.Index([1, 2, 3]).take([0, -1], allow_fill=True, fill_value=99)
ValueError: Unable to fill values because Index cannot contain NA
```

The caller provided a valid fill value that the dtype can hold, but `Index.take` rejects it because `_can_hold_na` is False for integer dtypes.

### Consequences

These force internal callers to bypass `Index.take` and work on the underlying arrays directly:

- **`frame.py` idxmin/idxmax**: `algorithms.take(index._values, ...)` instead of `index.take(...)`
- **`reshape/merge.py`**: appends a sentinel value to the index, with a comment: *"We do not use allow_fill and fill_value because it throws a ValueError on integer indices"*
- **`indexes/base.py` reset_index**: take-then-putmask as two operations
- **`io/formats/excel.py`**: guards `allow_fill` on `levels._can_hold_na`
- **`indexes/multi.py`**: `algos.take_nd(lev._values, ...)` instead of `lev.take(...)`

### Proposed fix

- Respect the caller's `fill_value`
- Remove the `_can_hold_na` gate (let the underlying array handle type promotion)
- Simplify the workaround sites

This is backward-compatible: the existing gate (`allow_fill=True` + `fill_value is None` → numpy-style take) is preserved, so bare `idx.take(indices)` is unchanged.

Separately, there are questions about the right long-term defaults for `allow_fill` (currently `True` for backward compat but arguably should be `False` to match `ExtensionArray.take`), but that would require a deprecation cycle and is out of scope here.

train.title: ENH: Simplify reading vertically stacked CSV tables
train.body:
### Feature Type

- [x] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [x] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

The overall goal is reading vertically stacked CSV files, with multiple tables.
There is no difficulty in writing such a file with pandas (just append) or reading and splitting horizontally stacked CSV files (but they can be inefficient and more complicated to write).
This is not technically a CSV format (according to RFC 4180, since column sizes differ) but a very slight generalisation of it.
It doesn't really have a name, but has been re-invented several times, with different ways of determining where to split the table.

I think the only form that really needs supporting are known specified lines, e.g. [[''], ['Col1', 'Col2']] would split on blank rows but also on Col1,Col2 rows. I had considered "when the number of columns changes", but I think that's a strictly less useful format (you can't have multiple tables with the same number of columns consecutively), and it could be extended in later if wanted.

### Feature Description

Possible solutions I can think of (any one of the following):
#### A) Part of TextFileReader chunking
   
   This would require the ability to reset the columns state of the reader (either by the user or as part of the implementation).
   If that is easy to do, then this might be the most straightforward way of implementing this feature.

   The simplest way of doing this is adding an option chunk_on = None, which can be set to a list of row values (permitted to include the blank row).
   Importantly the presence of this does not just cause the chunks to be broken off but also the number, header, names and types of columns to be reset (if not specified as a parameter) as if reading a new file. (But it does not reset if chunking because of chunksize, so the two are compatible.)

   If skip_blank_lines is True, then blank lines can end (if [''] is in chunk_on) but not begin or contribute to a chunk.
   I.e. consecutive skipped blank lines do not lead to 1x1 NA chunks, do not lead to 1x1 NAs before EOF or before other chunk_on rows, and do not lead to 1xN NA rows in previous or following chunks.
 

   If skip_blank_lines is False, then a blank line is interpreted as a row [''] and behaves the same as any other row (perhaps aside from NA conversion).
   If skip_blank_lines is True and [''] is not in chunk_on, then it is as if reading the file without blank lines in.
   (This should be the same as currently, aside from the new parameter cases.)

   Usage would look something like this
   ```CSV
   X,Y
   1,2
   3,4
   A,B,C
   x,y,3
   u,v,2
   ```

   ```Python
   xy = ['X', 'Y']
   abc = ['A', 'B', 'C']
   tables = {}

   for chunk in pd.read_csv(…, iterator=True, chunk_on = [xy, abc]):
       # header row 
       key = list(chunk.columns)
       # I don't actually know if omitting chunksize but keeping iterator leads to some implicit chunking.
       # If it doesn't then this can be simpler, not saying that it should though.
       # Also this example would concatenate repeated heading tables (but that's not a limitation of the interface)
       stored = tables.setdefault(key, chunk)
       if stored is not chunk:
           tables[key] = pd.concat(stored, chunk, ignore_index = True)

   >>> tables[xy]
      X  Y # int, int
   0  1  2
   1  3  4

   >>> tables[abc]
      A  B  C # str, str, int
   0  x  y  3
   1  u  v  2
   ```


#### B) Implement a function to directly read vertically stacked CSV (or an parameter read_csv is overloaded with).
   This is the simplest and fastest from the user's perspective but possibly the least convenient to implement, and raises many questions about the interface. This could return an iterable (forward compatible if changed to some object type) of the distinct tables.

   One option that might not cost much in terms of implementation is to convert the existing read_csv implementation

train.body:
### Pandas version checks

### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd
pd.to_timedelta([1.0, 1.01], unit="s")
```

### Issue Description

`pd.to_timedelta()` does ignore the unit argument in certain cases.

For the example above we get in `pandas<3.0`:

TimedeltaIndex(['0 days 00:00:01', '0 days 00:00:01.010000'], dtype='timedelta64[ns]', freq=None)

Most likely it was introduced by #63533

train.title: ENH: Add DataFrame.memory_report() for actionable dtype optimization suggestions
train.body: ### Feature Type - [x] Adding new functionality to pandas - [ ] Changing existing functionality in pandas - [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas ### Problem Description DataFrame.memory_usage() tells you how much memory a DataFrame uses, but gives no guidance on why or what to do about it. Users who want to optimize memory must: - Manually inspect each column's dtype - Know the integer/float downcast rules by heart - Manually check cardinality for object columns - Write their own loops to apply changes This is a very common pain point — especially for data engineers and analysts working with medium-to-large datasets who hit memory pressure and have no built-in tool to diagnose it. ### Feature Description A new method DataFrame.memory_report() that: 1. Analyzes every column's current dtype and actual value range 2. Suggests the smallest safe dtype for each column 3. Explains why each suggestion is safe (value range, cardinality ratio) 4. Returns a rich MemoryReport object that is both human-readable and 5. machine-readable 6. Never modifies the DataFrame — purely diagnostic, zero side effects def memory_report( self, verbose: bool = True, category_threshold: float = 0.5, check_datetimes: bool = True, ) -> MemoryReport: """ Analyze memory usage and suggest safe dtype optimizations. Parameters ---------- verbose : bool, default True If True, print the full report to stdout. category_threshold : float, default 0.5 Suggest ``category`` dtype when unique ratio is below this value. For example, 0.5 means fewer than 50% unique values → suggest category. check_datetimes : bool, default True Attempt to detect datetime-parseable strings in object columns. Samples up to 200 rows to avoid scanning very large columns. Returns ------- MemoryReport Structured report with per-column diagnostics. Supports: - ``report.to_dataframe()`` — machine-readable table - ``report.apply(df)`` — apply all suggestions, returns new df - ``report.actionable`` — list of columns with suggestions - ``report.high_impact`` — columns with >= 50% savings potential """ ### Alternative Solutions df.info(memory_usage='deep'). This is the closest native.But no guidance on how to fix it. ### Additional Context Design Decisions Zero side effects. memory_report() never modifies the DataFrame. Applying suggestions is always an explicit opt-in via report.apply(df). Safe-only suggestions. Every suggestion is lossless by default: Integer downcasts are validated against actual min/max values Float32 suggestions are validated: values are cast to float32 and checked for overflow before recommending apply() wraps each conversion in a try/except and warns on failure — it never raises Null awareness. The report flags columns with nulls so users know before applying dtype changes that may affect null representation. Overflow guard for floats. The implementation detects when a finite float64 value would become ±inf after float32 cast, and keeps float64. Composable return type. Returning a MemoryReport rather than just printing means the output is usable in notebooks, CI pipelines, and data quality checks.

train.title: BUG: Regression - `df[key] = df[key] / x` silently drops assignment on MultiIndex columns with mixed-dtype level and single sub-column
train.body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

cols = pd.MultiIndex.from_tuples(
    [('info', 'M'), ('info', 0),
     ('earnings', 1), ('earnings', 2),
     ('prices', 0)]
)
df = pd.DataFrame(
    np.arange(20, dtype=float).reshape(4, 5),
    columns=cols,
)

df['earnings'] = df['earnings'] / 100   # works
df['prices']   = df['prices']   / 100   # silent no-op — no error, no warning

print(df)
#    info       earnings       prices
#       M     0        1     2      0
# 0   0.0   1.0     0.02  0.03    4.0
# 1   5.0   6.0     0.07  0.08    9.0
# 2  10.0  11.0     0.12  0.13   14.0
# 3  15.0  16.0     0.17  0.18   19.0
#
# 'earnings' was divided by 100; 'prices' was not.
```

### Issue Description

> _Disclaimer: In writing this bug report I have used AI. This bug was found because the same code has a different behaviour in version 2.2.3 as in 3.0.1. I have verified the reproducible example in both latest versions, 2.3.3 vs. 3.0.2. I'm familiar with the copy on write changes, but I'm far from a pandas expert._

Top-level `__setitem__` on a column MultiIndex silently discards the assignment — no error, no warning — when all three of the following conditions hold:

1. The DataFrame has a column MultiIndex.
2. The second level has `object` dtype due to mixed element types. In the example above, `'M'` (string) is on level 1 alongside integers `0, 1, 2`, which forces `df.columns.levels[1]` to `object`.
3. The top-level label being assigned to contains exactly **one** sub-column (here `('prices', 0)`). Top-level labels with multiple sub-columns (here `earnings` with `1` and `2`) are assigned correctly.

I isolated the trigger by varying level 1:

| level 1                          | multi sub-col (`earnings`) | single sub-col (`prices`) |
|----------------------------------|----------------------------|---------------------------|
| all int `[0, 1, 2]`              | ✅ divided                  | ✅ divided                 |
| all string `['M', '0', '1', '2']`| ✅ divided                  | ✅ divided                 |
| **mixed `[0, 1, 2, 'M']`**       | ✅ divided                  | ❌ silent no-op            |

So the bug is specifically the combination of an object-dtype level and a single-element top-level group going through the frame-assignment path.

This is a **regression from 2.3.3 → 3.0.x**. The same code divides `prices` correctly on 2.3.3 and silently drops the write on 3.0.2.

Workarounds that do work on 3.0.2:

```python
df[('prices', 0)] = df[('prices', 0)] / 100          # tuple form — OK
df.loc[:, ('prices', 0)] = df.loc[:, ('prices', 0)] / 100   # OK
```

Workarounds that also silently fail or corrupt data on 3.0.2:

```python
df['prices'] /= 100                                   # silent no-op
df.loc[:, 'prices'] = df.loc[:, 'prices'] / 100       # fills 'prices' with NaN
```

Given this is silent data loss on a plain (non-chained) `__setitem__`, it seems clearly unintended rather than a CoW semantic change.

### Expected Behavior

`df['prices'] = df['prices'] / 100` should either divide the values in place, raise, or warn. It should not silently discard the assignment. The presence of a string label elsewhere on level 1, or the number of sub-columns under the selected top-level label, should not affect whether the assignment takes effect.

My own verification:

train.title: BUG: Regression when using `.str[...]` accessor on `ArrowExtensionArray`
train.body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
>>> import pandas as pd
>>> x = pd.Series(["abc"])
>>> x.str[0]
0    a
dtype: str
>>> x_converted = x.convert_dtypes(dtype_backend="pyarrow")
>>> x_converted.str[0]
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<python-input-4>", line 1, in <module>
    x_converted.str[0]
    ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~^^^
  File "...\pandas\core\strings\accessor.py", line 254, in __getitem__
    result = self._data.array._str_getitem(key)
             ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
AttributeError: 'ArrowExtensionArray' object has no attribute '_str_getitem'. Did you mean: '_str_istitle'?
```

### Issue Description

When using `.convert_dtypes(dtype_backend="pyarrow")`, the underlying array of string types is an `ArrowExtensionArray`. Previously, this class inherited string methods from `ArrowStringArrayMixin` and `BaseStringArrayMethods`. However, in 3.0.0, that was changed to remove `BaseStringArrayMethods` (#62155).

Unfortunately, `BaseStringArrayMethods` does not have full parity with `ArrowStringArrayMixin`. I did a quick search of the other differences, and `_str_getitem` appears to be the only difference that causes this problem.

I think `ArrowStringArrayMixin` or `ArrowExtensionArray` should implement the `_str_getitem` method, though another solution would be to have `.convert_dtypes(dtype_backend="pyarrow")` to produce an `ArrayStringArray` instead of an `ArrowExtensionArray` for string columns. I'm not familiar enough with the details of these types to know why we would prefer the latter.

### Expected Behavior

`x.str[0]` works for any string-typed `x`

```python
import pandas as pd
  import adbc_driver_sqlite.dbapi as adbc_sqlite
                                                                                                                        
  conn = adbc_sqlite.connect(":memory:")                                                                                
                                                                                                                        
  # Create two tables                                                                                                   
  pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2, 3], "name": ["Alice", "Bob", "Charlie"]}).to_sql(                                        
      "users", conn, if_exists="replace", index=False                                                                   
  )
  pd.DataFrame({"secret": ["password123", "api_key"]}).to_sql(                                                          
      "audit_log", conn, if_exists="replace", index=False                                                               
  )
                                                                                                                        
  # Attacker controls the `name` parameter — targets a different table                                                  
  from pandas.io.sql import ADBCDatabase
  db = ADBCDatabase(conn)                                                                                               
                                                                                                                      
  # Capture the SQL that delete_rows generates                                                                          
  import unittest.mock as mock                                                                                        
  with mock.patch.object(db, "execute", wraps=db.execute) as m:                                                         
      db.delete_rows("audit_log")   # attacker-controlled name                                                        
      print("SQL generated:", m.call_args[0][0])                                                                        
      # Output: DELETE FROM audit_log                                                                                   
      # → all rows deleted from "audit_log" even though caller intended "users"                                         
                                                                                                                        
  # With multi-statement payload (driver-dependent):                                                                    
  malicious = 'users; DROP TABLE audit_log; --'                                                                         
  table_name = malicious   # exactly what ADBCDatabase.delete_rows builds                                               
  print(f"Injected SQL: DELETE FROM {table_name}")                                                                      
  # Output: DELETE FROM users; DROP TABLE audit_log; --

train.title: DOC: Clarify rolling window behavior with negative offset strings and froward rolling windows
train.body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that the issue still exists on the latest versions of the docs on `main` [here](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/)


### Location of the documentation

https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.Series.rolling.html
https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.rolling.html

### Documentation problem

There is no documentation on a forward-looking rolling windows with offset strings.
I often need to make a forward-looking rolling window on datetime data. To do so, I've tried different ways and the only one I found was using two `.iloc[::-1]` (reverse the series order) with the rolling occurring in the middle. 

nb: Because the data has irregular DateTimeIndex (not every 2 hours for example), I can not use the `pd.api.indexers.FixedForwardWindowIndexer` 

```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

fake_data = [1, 5, 4, 6, 7, 65, 21, 5, np.nan, 56, 1]
random_index = pd.to_datetime([
    '2025-01-01 00:22:00', '2025-01-01 02:31:00',
    '2025-01-01 05:00:00', '2025-01-01 07:18:00',
    '2025-01-01 09:42:00', '2025-01-01 12:29:00',
    '2025-01-01 14:38:00', '2025-01-01 16:59:00',
    '2025-01-01 19:32:00', '2025-01-01 22:03:00',
    '2025-01-02 00:25:00'
])
ser = pd.Series(fake_data, index=random_index)

out = pd.DataFrame({
    "raw": ser,
    "5h": ser.rolling("5h").max(),
    "-5h": ser.rolling("-5h").max(),
    "5h_inv": ser.iloc[::-1].rolling("5h").max().iloc[::-1],
    "-5h_inv": ser.iloc[::-1].rolling("-5h").max().iloc[::-1],
})
print(out)
```

2025-01-01 16:59:00   5.0  65.0   5.0     5.0      5.0
2025-01-01 19:32:00   NaN  21.0   NaN    56.0      NaN
2025-01-01 22:03:00  56.0  56.0  56.0    56.0     56.0
2025-01-02 00:25:00   1.0  56.0   1.0     1.0      1.0
```

This is what this shows :
- The behavior of negative offset strings (e.g., "-5h") in Series.rolling() and DataFrame.rolling() is not documented and produces counterintuitive results. They don't inverse the rolling window, the window just collaps into 1 element windows. The negative int values are actually prohibited by the function (`ValueError: window must be an integer 0 or greater`) so I would expect the same to be for offset stings. > Maybe a bug ?

- Using .iloc[::-1] to invert the series before performing the rolling window (suggested by https://stackoverflow.com/questions/51740121/pandas-rolling-how-to-roll-from-left-to-right-or-from-up-to-down) works. But, you still have to use a positive offset even if your dataset is anticrhonological order when the rolling occurs.


### Suggested fix for documentation

For me, adding something like the following text on the examples (https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/v3.0.2/pandas/core/generic.py#L12058-L12109) would do the tricks:

        Rolling sum with forward-looking windows with 3 seconds

        >>> df_time.iloc[::-1].rolling("3s").sum().iloc[::-1]
                       B
        2013-01-01 09:00:00  1.0
        2013-01-01 09:00:02  3.0
        2013-01-01 09:00:03  2.0
        2013-01-01 09:00:05  4.0
        2013-01-01 09:00:06  4.0

        Note: Negative offset strings (e.g., ``"-5h"``) do not create forward-looking
        windows and should be avoided. They collapse to single-element windows.

train.title: ENH/BUG: Utilize `_values_for_json` in `Series.to_json`
train.body:
### Feature Type

- [x] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [x] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

ExtensionArrays can define a `_values_for_json` method if the standard numpy array with `object` dtype returned by `__array__` is not serializable because the objects themselves are not serializable. However this method is only utilized for `DataFrame.to_json` trough `BlockManager.column_arrays`:

https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/353763e607745e6fad90fed89efe97bd1f87ebae/pandas/core/internals/managers.py#L1249-L1251

In `Series.to_json` no path leads to the `_values_for_json` method and nearly always `__array__` is utilized. Therefore some ExtensionArrays are only JSON serializable if they are in a `DataFrame` and not a `Series`, which in my opinion also could be considered a bug.

### Feature Description

In short modify the `objToJSON.c` file to also call `_values_for_json` for pandas `Series`.

With the help of GitHub Copilot I was able to trace the issue to the `get_values` function, specifically the following lines:
https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/353763e607745e6fad90fed89efe97bd1f87ebae/pandas/_libs/src/vendored/ujson/python/objToJSON.c#L201-L213

- In `201` we are effectively calling `Series.values` and assign it to `values`.
- If the `Series` and therefore `values` is not empty `values` now is a numpy array or ExtensionArray.
- Next in `205` it is checked if `values` has a `__array__` attribute and if so calls it, that is also the path mentioned above that leads potentially to the numpy array of object dtype with not serializable objects in it.
- At last in `210` if none of the checks above worked it is checked if `values` is already a `np.ndarray` (and only that, so no subclass) and if not dereferences `values` and tries to create the array somewhere up the stack (if I understand it correctly).

My proposal would be to add another check after the empty check but before the `__array__` check. Similar to the `__array__` check it could test if `values` has a `_values_for_json` attribute (and therefore is an ExtensionArray) and if so calls that method to create the serializable numpy array. This check could work like the following snippet, but I have not tried it out yet. It would be important to include it before the `__array__` check as ExtensionArrays have that attribute too:
```c
else if (PyObject_HasAttrString(values, "_values_for_json")) {
    // We have gotten an ExtensionArray
    PyObject *array_values = PyObject_CallMethod(values, "_values_for_json", NULL);
    Py_DECREF(values);
    values = array_values;
}
```
Disclaimer: This snipped was developed with GitHub Copilot after chatting with it to understand how the `get_values` function works and asking if a check similar to `__array__` would also work in the designated spot. It also suggested to not make it an `else if` block but an `if` block so that if the return value of `_values_for_json` itself is not already a `np.ndarray` but an array-like object the following checks could still convert that object using the `__array__` attribute. In my opinion that is not necessary because the function signature of `_values_for_json` already specifies that the return value shall be a `np.ndarray` and the base implementation just calls `np.asarray(self)` which should also dispatch to `__array__`. I therefore modified the snipped above accordingly. As there currently do not seem to be any test for `_values_for_json`, adding tests that make sure that this method actually returns an `np.ndarray` and that the values inside are serializable seems sensible.

### Alternative Solutions

Always convert your `Series` to `DataFrame` with `sr.to_frame()` before JSON serialization, then the `_values_for_json` method of the ExtensionArray is already used.

### Additional Context

I found this issue during my work for an external ExtensionArray to support astropy `Quantity` objects which

train.title: PERF: DataFrame row-wise .loc assignment is much slower with string_storage="pyarrow" than "python"
train.body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import time

import pandas as pd
import pyarrow as pa


def bench(storage: str, rows: int = 1000, cols: int = 20) -> float:
    pd.options.mode.string_storage = storage

    source = pd.DataFrame(
        [[f"v{j % 10}" for j in range(cols)] for _ in range(rows)]
    ).astype(str)
    out = pd.DataFrame(columns=source.columns).astype(str)

    start = time.perf_counter()
    for i, row in enumerate(source.itertuples(index=False)):
        out.loc[i] = row
    return time.perf_counter() - start


print(f"pandas={pd.__version__} pyarrow={pa.__version__}")
for storage in ("python", "pyarrow"):
    elapsed = bench(storage)
    print(storage, elapsed)
```

### Issue Description

I mentioned this to the arrow devs as well: https://github.com/apache/arrow/issues/49612

`pd.options.mode.string_storage = "pyarrow"` causes a large slowdown when repeatedly growing a string-typed `DataFrame` with `loc` row assignment.

The performance issue largely goes away if I switch to:

```python
pd.options.mode.string_storage = "python"
```

### Expected Behavior


```text
pandas=3.0.1 pyarrow=23.0.1 rows=1000 cols=20
storage=python  array=StringArray       seconds=0.420
storage=pyarrow array=ArrowStringArray  seconds=3.316
slowdown(pyarrow/python)=7.89x
```

I also see the same pattern with smaller sizes, for example:

```text
500x10:  python=0.147s  pyarrow=0.508s
500x20:  python=0.200s  pyarrow=0.930s
1000x10: python=0.292s  pyarrow=1.759s

```text

```

train.title: DOC: Clarify Series index alignment in DataFrame.assign
train.body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that the issue still exists on the latest versions of the docs on `main` [here](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/)


### Location of the documentation

https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.assign.html

### Documentation problem

The current `DataFrame.assign()` documentation states that non-callable values such as a Series, scalar, or array are "simply assigned." However, it does not clearly explain that when a Series is passed, values are aligned by index labels rather than by position.

This behavior may be surprising to users, especially when compared to list or ndarray assignment, which is positional.

### Suggested fix for documentation

Add a short clarification and example demonstrating that:

- Series values are aligned by index labels
- Missing labels result in NaN values
- List/ndarray values are assigned positionally

train.title: BUG: dtype check fails for `object` due to being `NumpyEADtype` in `frame.to_series`
train.body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

### Reproducible Example

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

arr = pd.array(["a", "b", np.nan, np.nan], dtype=object)
print(type(getattr(arr, "dtype", None)))  # NumpyEADtype, not default object
print(getattr(arr, "dtype", None) == object)  # returns false
```

### Issue Description

`getattr(arr, "dtype", None) == object` returns `false` due to being a `NumpyEADtype`, when is should return `true`.

The check is used in `frame.to_series` to assign the correct dtype when running the function. Currently causes errors down the line when summing frames with the type of `object` due to dtype not being assigned correctly.

train.title: ENH: add method="time" to .reindex() to interpolate timeseries to different DatetimeIndex
train.body:
### Feature Type

- [x] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [ ] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

I have searched for existing issues, but can find none that covers this case, although I cannot imagine someone else did not already report this. Please feel free to close this issue as duplicated if that is the case anyway.

Converting an irregularly-spaced datetime-indexed Series/DataFrame to a fixed frequency with time-aware interpolation requires a multi-step operation (`reindex` + `union` + `sort_index` + `interpolate` + `reindex`). This is a common use case for time series data (water level measurements in my case) but lacks a dedicated, elegant pandas method.


### Feature Description

My ideal new method would look like this:
```
fixed = water_level.reindex(new_index, method="time")
```

However, `method="time"` is not available in `reindex()`. I also tried `.resample()`, but that is not for interpolating between values, but aggregating the data in bins, which is not what I am looking for here.


### Alternative Solutions

As far as I know (and as far as Claude knows), this is the most elegant way to do what I need in pandas at the moment:
```python
import pandas as pd

def interpolate_to_fixed_freq(series, freq):
    """Convert irregular time series to fixed frequency with time-aware interpolation."""
    new_index = pd.date_range(start=series.index.min(), end=series.index.max(), freq=freq)
    return (series
            .reindex(series.index.union(new_index))
            .sort_index()
            .interpolate(method='time')
            .reindex(new_index))

# Example: irregular water level measurements
idx = pd.to_datetime(['2024-01-01 00:00', '2024-01-01 00:07',
                      '2024-01-01 00:22', '2024-01-01 01:05'])
water_level = pd.Series([1.0, 1.5, 2.3, 3.1], index=idx, name='level_m')

# Convert to 15-minute fixed frequency
fixed = interpolate_to_fixed_freq(water_level, '15min')
print(fixed)
```

Gives the desired behaviour:
```
2024-01-01 00:00:00    1.000000
2024-01-01 00:15:00    1.926667
2024-01-01 00:30:00    2.448837
2024-01-01 00:45:00    2.727907
2024-01-01 01:00:00    3.006977
Freq: 15min, Name: level_m, dtype: float64
```



### Additional Context

This example is for going from going from a irregular to a regular spaced DatetimeIndex, but of course this goes for interpolating to any DatetimeIndex.

train.title: ENH: Add coerce errors functionality to pandas.Series.apply
train.body:
### Feature Type

- [ ] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [x] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

I would like to use pandas.Series.apply without creating helper functions to coerce errors. 

Currently if I am applying a function to a series that I know could raise errors (for example, trying to make each item in series of strings into an int), I have to write a small helper function to coerce errors into None or other.

I would like pandas.Series.apply to have a new parameter called errors, with possible values of 'raise' and 'coerce', similar to pandas.to_datetime.


### Feature Description

Adds a new parameter to pandas.Series.apply, to coerce errors.

Pseudocode implementation:
```
def apply(self):
    func = self.func
    if self.errors == "coerce":
        def safe_func(val):
            try:
                return func(val)
            except Exception:
                return np.nan
        results = [safe_func(val) for val in self.values]
    else:
        results = [func(val) for val in self.values]
    return results
```

Example usage:
```
s = pandas.Series(['1', '2', 'N/A'])
s = s.apply(lambda x: int(x), errors = 'coerce')
```

### Alternative Solutions

Write helper functions when necessary:
```
def coerce_to_int(x):
    try: return int(x)
    except: return None
s = pandas.Series(['1', '2', 'N/A'])
s = s.apply(coerce_to_int)
```

This is viable but requires the user to write many helper functions. 

### Additional Context

train.title: BUG: No longer possible to assign `attrs` to pandas column
train.body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
df = pd.DataFrame({"A": [1, 2], "B": [3, 4]})
df.attrs = {"A": [10, 20, 30]}
df['A'].attrs['info'] = 'Antofagasta'
df['A'].attrs
```

### Issue Description

While it is possible to assign metadata to dataframes, it appears that it is no longer possible to assign metadata to columns.

The column will simply inherit the `attrs` of the dataframe.

The good part is that the `attrs` of the dataframe seem to remain in place after modifying it (e.g. by dropping rows), which didn't hold in version `2.3.3` for instance.

---
I wanted to look through the code, but it appears that [[source]](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/v3.0.1+1.g304fd2b639/pandas/core/generic.py#L318-L354) on the [pandas.DataFrame.attrs](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.attrs.html) page points to a non-existing location.

### Expected Behavior

The output of `df['A'].attrs` from above should be `{'info': 'Antofagasta'}`. And this information should remain when the dataframe is modified, e.g. when rows or other columns are dropped, when the index is changed, when another dataframe is merged into the current one, etc.

train.title: BUG: mask(inplace=True) gives where() results in EA recursive path
train.body:
`DataFrame.mask(cond, other, axis, inplace=True)` produces incorrect results (equivalent to `where()`) when `other` is a Series with ExtensionArray values.

```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

df = pd.DataFrame({"A": [1, 2, 3], "B": [4, 5, 6]})
ser = pd.Series(pd.array([7, pd.NA, 9]))
mask = np.ones(df.shape, dtype=bool)
mask[1, :] = False

df.mask(mask, ser, axis=0)            # correct: replaces rows 0, 2
df.mask(mask, ser, axis=0, inplace=True)  # wrong: replaces row 1 (where() semantics)
```

The cause is a double negation in `NDFrame._where`. `mask()` passes `~cond`, then `_where` negates again (`cond = -cond if inplace`) before reaching the EA recursive path at `generic.py:10095-10120`. The recursive `_where` calls are non-inplace, so they interpret the double-negated cond with where semantics, producing the wrong result.

The non-EA path (which goes through `putmask`) is not affected.

train.title: ENH: Proposal for pd.col() for multi-column and regex column selection
train.body:
### Feature Type

- [x] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [ ] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

`pd.col()` currently only supports selecting a **single column**, even though its
behavior allows expressions to be chained in ways that naturally suggest
multi-column operations should also work.

The function is defined as:

```python
def col(col_name: Hashable) -> Expression:
```

Internally it constructs an `Expression` whose evaluation function does:

```python
def func(df: DataFrame) -> Series:
    if col_name not in df.columns:
        raise ValueError(...)
    return df[col_name]
```

This always returns a **Series**, meaning `pd.col()` is fundamentally
single-column oriented.

### Inconsistent behavior with lists

Passing a list currently does not raise a clear error:

```python
pd.col(["price", "discount"])
```

The expression is created successfully, but when evaluated it produces:

```python
df[["price", "discount"]]   # returns a DataFrame
```

This creates inconsistent behavior when chaining operations such as:

```python
df.assign(total=pd.col(["price", "discount"]).sum())
```

because the expression now operates on a **DataFrame instead of a Series**.
The behavior becomes unclear and differs from user expectations.

### Missing regex selection

There is currently no way to express pattern-based column selection inside
`pd.col()`:

```python
pd.col("^price_", regex=True)
```

This fails with:

```python
TypeError: col() got an unexpected keyword argument 'regex'
```

Users must instead rely on eager operations such as:

```python
df.filter(regex="^price_")
```

which breaks the composable expression style that `pd.col()` aims to provide.

### Summary of limitations

Currently `pd.col()` does **not support**:

- Multi-column selection
- Regex-based column selection
- dtype-based column selection
- Any expression whose base resolves to a DataFrame

This limits the usefulness of the expression API for many real-world workflows.


### Feature Description

Extend `pd.col()` so it can reference **multiple columns and column groups**
while still returning an `Expression`.

### Proposed signature

```python
def col(
    col_name: Hashable | list[Hashable] | None = None,
    *,
    regex: str | None = None,
    dtype: str | type | None = None,
) -> Expression:
```

### Behavior

1. **Single column (current behavior)**

```python
pd.col("price")
```

Resolves to:

```python
df["price"]   # Series
```

2. **Multi-column list**

```python
pd.col(["price", "discount"])
```

Resolves to:

```python
df[["price", "discount"]]   # DataFrame
```

which enables operations like:

```python
df.assign(
    total=pd.col(["price", "discount"]).sum(axis=1)
)
```

3. **Regex selection**

```python
pd.col(regex="^price_")
```

Resolves to:

```python
df.filter(regex="^price_")
```

Example usage:

```python
df.assign(
    total_price=pd.col(regex="^price_").sum(axis=1)
)
```

4. **dtype selection**

```python
pd.col(dtype="float64")
```

Resolves to:

```python
df.select_dtypes(include="float64")
```

### Why this works with the existing Expression system

The `Expression` evaluation pipeline already supports this:

```python
result = expr._eval_expression(df)
```

If the base expression returns a **DataFrame**, chained operations like
`.sum(axis=1)` naturally return a **Series**, which is compatible with
`assign`, `loc`, and other pandas APIs.

Example:

```python
df.assign(
    total=pd.col(["a", "b"]).sum(axis=1)
)
```

The final expression resolves to a Series and integrates seamlessly
with the existing execution flow.

### Alternative Solutions


Without this feature, users must fall back to less expressive patterns.

### Lambda workaround

The most common workaround is using a lambda:

```python
df.assign(
    total=lambda df: df[["price", "discount"]].sum(axis=1)
)
```

While functional, this approach has drawbacks:

- Lambdas are not reusable

## Issue

In `pandas/io/stata.py` line 285, the `parse_dates_safe` function uses `Series.apply` with a lambda to extract year and month from object-dtype datetime columns:

year_month = dates.apply(lambda x: 100 * x.year + x.month)

d["year"] = date_index._data.year

train.title: BUG: Plotting with duplicate column names gives misleading error
train.body:
### Pandas version checks

- [X] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.
- [X] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3], "b": [4, 5, 6]})
df.columns = ["a", "a"]

df.plot.hist()
# TypeError: no numeric data to plot

df.plot.box()
# TypeError: no numeric data to plot
```

### Issue Description

Plotting a DataFrame with duplicate column names raises `TypeError: no numeric data to plot`, even when all columns are numeric.

The root cause is in `MPLPlot.__init__` ([core.py line 193-195](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/main/pandas/plotting/_matplotlib/core.py#L193-L195)):

```python
self.columns = [
    col for col in data.columns if is_numeric_dtype(data[col])
]
```

When columns are non-unique, `data[col]` returns a DataFrame instead of a Series. `is_numeric_dtype` returns `False` for DataFrames, so all duplicate-named columns are silently dropped, leaving `self.columns` empty.

Even if this filter were fixed (e.g. using positional indexing), duplicate column names would still break downstream in multiple places:

- `_ensure_frame` (line ~681): `data.loc[:, cols]` with duplicate names causes column expansion
- `_get_nseries` (line ~507): `len(self.columns)` double-counts duplicate names
- `_compute_plot_data` (line ~691): passes duplicate labels into `reconstruct_data_with_by` → `MultiIndex.from_product`, multiplying the problem
- Scatter/hexbin plots (lines ~1352, 1395): `data[x]`/`data[y]` return DataFrames instead of Series, breaking shape expectations

The plotting pipeline fundamentally relies on label-based indexing (`data[col]`, `data.loc[:, cols]`) at every stage, so duplicate columns can't work without significant rework.

### Expected Behavior

Either:
1. Raise a clear error early (e.g. `ValueError: plotting requires unique column names`), or
2. Handle duplicate columns correctly throughout the pipeline

Option 1 seems most practical given how pervasive the label-based indexing is.

train.title: BUG: Assigning pd.NA to ArrowStringArray after 3-way slice concat silently corrupts other rows
train.body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd
import pyarrow as pa
import platform

print("=== VERSIONS ===")
print(f"Python:   {platform.python_version()}")
print(f"Pandas:   {pd.__version__}")
print(f"PyArrow:  {pa.__version__}")

base1 = pd.DataFrame({"a": ["short"] * 10, "b": ["x"] * 10})
base2 = pd.DataFrame({"a": ["short"] * 10, "b": ["x"] * 10})
base1["id"] = range(10)
base2["id"] = range(10, 20)

new_row = pd.DataFrame({"a": ["NEW_ROW"], "b": ["x"], "id": [-1]})
split_idx = 5

print()
print("=== 3-WAY CONCAT + NULL ASSIGNMENT (buggy) ===")
df_3way = pd.concat([base1, base2], ignore_index=True)
df_3way = pd.concat([
    df_3way.iloc[:split_idx],
    new_row,
    df_3way.iloc[split_idx:]
], ignore_index=True)
df_3way.loc[[0], "a"] = pd.NA
print(df_3way.to_string())

print()
print("=== 3-WAY CONCAT + STRING ASSIGNMENT (works fine) ===")
df_3way_str = pd.concat([base1, base2], ignore_index=True)
df_3way_str = pd.concat([
    df_3way_str.iloc[:split_idx],
    new_row,
    df_3way_str.iloc[split_idx:]
], ignore_index=True)
df_3way_str.loc[[0], "a"] = "something"
print(df_3way_str.to_string())

print()
print("=== 2-WAY CONCAT + NULL ASSIGNMENT (safe workaround) ===")
df_2way = pd.concat([base1, base2], ignore_index=True)
df_2way["sort"] = range(len(df_2way))
new_row2 = pd.DataFrame({"a": ["NEW_ROW"], "b": ["x"], "id": [-1], "sort": [split_idx + 0.5]})
df_2way = (
    pd.concat([df_2way, new_row2], ignore_index=True)
    .sort_values("sort")
    .reset_index(drop=True)
)
df_2way.loc[[0], "a"] = pd.NA
print(df_2way.to_string())
```

### Issue Description

When inserting a row at a specific position using a 3-way slice concat, subsequent assignment of `pd.NA` to a string column silently corrupts some rows.

In the buggy case, rows 6–10 (ids 5–9) have their `a` value silently wiped to empty string despite not being part of the assignment. The `b` and `id` columns in those same rows are completely unaffected, confirming the corruption is isolated to the Arrow string column.

Two comparisons are included to narrow down the cause:

- **3-way concat + regular string assignment** works correctly, showing the bug is specific to null assignment
- **2-way concat + null assignment** works correctly, showing the bug is specific to the 3-chunk structure created by the slice

No exception is raised — the corruption is completely silent, making it particularly dangerous in production code.

This may be related to #64320 but distinct in that the corruption manifests as silent data loss rather than an exception, and is triggered by a 3-chunk structure rather than a 2-chunk structure.

train.title: DEPR: deprecate set_eng_float_format
train.body: Claude wrote this at my request. ## Proposal Deprecate `pd.set_eng_float_format()` in favor of using `pd.set_option("display.float_format", EngFormatter(...))` directly. Human Update Or just deprecate without an alternative. I haven't seen any evidence that anyone uses this. ## Rationale `set_eng_float_format` is a legacy convenience function (added in v0.5.0) that is a thin wrapper around `set_option`: ```python def set_eng_float_format(accuracy=3, use_eng_prefix=False): set_option("display.float_format", EngFormatter(accuracy, use_eng_prefix)) ``` It is the only top-level `pd.set_*` function that exists outside the options API, making it an odd outlier in the public API. This was already identified in #15610, where the consensus was to integrate this into the options machinery or deprecate it. **Evidence of minimal usage:** - **GitHub code search** yields ~30 results for `set_eng_float_format` outside pandas-dev/pandas. The vast majority are vendored copies of pandas, type stubs, or re-exports (xorbits, modin, Apache Beam, pyparallel, pandas-stubs, etc.). Only **2** results are actual user code calling this function. - **Stack Overflow** has **zero** questions or answers mentioning `set_eng_float_format`. - **Only 2 bug reports** have ever been filed against this function in the pandas issue tracker (#11981 in 2016, #15610 in 2017). The replacement is straightforward and equally concise: ```python # Before pd.set_eng_float_format(accuracy=3, use_eng_prefix=True) # After from pandas.io.formats.format import EngFormatter pd.set_option("display.float_format", EngFormatter(accuracy=3, use_eng_prefix=True)) ``` This keeps `EngFormatter` available (it is not being deprecated), removes a one-off top-level function that doesn't fit the options API pattern, and simplifies the public API surface. Closes #15610.

train.title: DOC: Public APIs missing from the API reference documentation
train.body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that the issue still exists on the latest versions of the docs on `main` [here](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/)


### Location of the documentation

https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/reference/index.html

### Documentation problem

The following 5 public APIs have docstrings in the source code but are not listed
in any `doc/source/reference/*.rst` file, so they do not appear in the rendered
API reference.

Found by comparing `dir()` output on core classes against the autosummary entries
parsed from `doc/source/reference/*.rst`, then filtering out aliases (e.g.
`divide`→`div`, `tolist`→`to_list`) and methods already documented via a
property or on a parent/sibling class (e.g. `Index.transpose` via `Index.T`).

### Series (2 items)

| API | Source | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `pandas.Series.divmod` | `pandas/core/series.py` | Element-wise integer division and modulo (binary operator `divmod`) |
| `pandas.Series.rdivmod` | `pandas/core/series.py` | Reverse integer division and modulo (binary operator `rdivmod`) |

Note: every other binary operator pair (`div`/`rdiv`, `mod`/`rmod`, `add`/`radd`,
etc.) is listed in the "Binary operator functions" section of `series.rst`.
`divmod` and `rdivmod` are the only pair missing.

### Timestamp (2 items)

| API | Source | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `pandas.Timestamp.fromisocalendar` | C extension (`_libs.tslibs.timestamps`) | Constructs a Timestamp from ISO year, week number, and weekday |
| `pandas.Timestamp.fromisoformat` | C extension (`_libs.tslibs.timestamps`) | Constructs a Timestamp from an ISO 8601 format string |

These are pandas-specific overrides of `datetime.datetime` class methods. Other
Timestamp constructors (`Timestamp.now`, `Timestamp.today`, `Timestamp.combine`,
etc.) are already documented in `indexing.rst`.

### Timedelta (1 item)

| API | Source | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `pandas.Timedelta.resolution_string` | `pandas/_libs/tslibs/timedeltas.pyx` | Returns a string representing the lowest timedelta resolution |

Other Timedelta properties (`components`, `days`, `seconds`, `nanoseconds`,
`resolution_string`'s companion `resolution`, etc.) are already listed in
`indexing.rst`.


### Suggested fix for documentation

1. Add `Series.divmod` and `Series.rdivmod` to `doc/source/reference/series.rst`
   under the "Binary operator functions" subsection, alongside `div`, `rdiv`,
   `mod`, `rmod`, etc.

2. Add `Timestamp.fromisocalendar` and `Timestamp.fromisoformat` to
   `doc/source/reference/indexing.rst` under the Timestamp section, alongside
   the existing constructors (`Timestamp.now`, `Timestamp.today`, etc.).

3. Add `Timedelta.resolution_string` to `doc/source/reference/indexing.rst`
   under the Timedelta properties subsection, alongside `resolution`, `days`,
   `seconds`, etc.

Each addition is a single line in the corresponding RST file. These could be
combined into one small PR.

**This is not sufficient.**

The issue appears in multiple places across the documentation (e.g., parameter descriptions and examples where {{ }} is rendered instead of { }). We should identify and fix the root cause or update all affected occurrences, otherwise the docs will remain inconsistent and continue to show invalid Python syntax in other sections.

Just in `reference/api/pandas.read_csv.html` ([link](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.read_csv.html)), there are at least:

- Parameter type description for `na_values` renders incorrectly as:  
  `dict of {{HashableIterable}}`.

- Enum values for `engine` render incorrectly as:  
  `engine {{‘c’, ‘python’, ‘pyarrow’}}`.

- Enum values for `quoting` render incorrectly as:  
  `{{0 or csv.QUOTE_MINIMAL, 1 or csv.QUOTE_ALL, ...}}`.

- Header renaming description renders placeholders incorrectly as:  
  `".{{count}}"`.

- Placeholder examples for unnamed columns render incorrectly as:  
  `"Unnamed: {{i}}"` and `"Unnamed: {{i}}_level_{{level}}"`.

- Several dictionary examples throughout the page use `{{ }}` instead of `{ }`, which makes the shown Python code invalid.

### Documentation problem

The issue appears in multiple places across the documentation (e.g., parameter descriptions and examples where `{{ }}` is rendered instead of `{ }`). We should identify and fix the root cause or update all affected occurrences; otherwise, the docs will remain inconsistent and continue to show invalid Python syntax in other sections.

Related to https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/64394.

Just in `reference/api/pandas.read_csv.html` ([link](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.read_csv.html)), there are at least:
- Double braces `{{ }}` appear in code examples instead of normal Python dict braces `{ }`, producing invalid syntax (e.g., `dtype={{"Value": float}}`).

- The `date_format` example also uses double braces:  
  `date_format={{"col 2": "%d/%m/%Y", "col 3": "%a %d %b %Y"}}`.

- Parameter type description for `dtype` renders incorrectly as:  
  `dict of {{Hashable dtype}}`.

- Parameter type description for `converters` renders incorrectly as:  
  `dict of {{HashableCallable}}`.

- Parameter type description for `na_values` renders incorrectly as:  
  `dict of {{HashableIterable}}`.

- Enum values for `engine` render incorrectly as:  
  `engine {{‘c’, ‘python’, ‘pyarrow’}}`.

- Enum values for `quoting` render incorrectly as:  
  `{{0 or csv.QUOTE_MINIMAL, 1 or csv.QUOTE_ALL, ...}}`.

- Header renaming description renders placeholders incorrectly as:  
  `".{{count}}"`.

- Placeholder examples for unnamed columns render incorrectly as:  
  `"Unnamed: {{i}}"` and `"Unnamed: {{i}}_level_{{level}}"`.

- Several dictionary examples throughout the page use `{{ }}` instead of `{ }`, which makes the shown Python code invalid.

### Suggested fix for documentation

I assume the double braces were originally used to escape literal `{}` in docstrings that passed through a .format()/Substitution step. Since the formatting step is seemingly no longer applied (TBC?) in the current doc build, the escapes now leak into the rendered docs, so they should be replaced across the repo with normal braces only if we can confirm they're no longer necessary or we need to fix the build step.

train.title: DEPR: float_precision in read_csv
train.body: We have "high" (the default), "legacy", and "round_trip". When it was introduced in #8044, using the "high" precision apparently came with a performance penalty, but that changed by 2017 (https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/17154#issuecomment-319917647) so the default was changed from "legacy" to "high" in #36228. I can't think of any reason why anyone would use "legacy". I'm not aware of anyone who uses this parameter at all. Let's deprecate it and simplify the code+API. Update: I patched the code to always use precision="high" to see whether it broke any tests. Aside from a test specifically asserting that "legacy" is _inaccurate_, the only test that broke was `test_precise_conversion` (4 cases out of 42) where we parse `1.700000000000000177635684` to `1.7`. I'm fine with this level of rounding (though I think using `fast_float` might improve it to `1.7000000000000002` which is what pyarrow gives). I'd also be OK with saying "round_trip" level precision is only for the python engine (though that engine also gives 1.7)

train.title: BUG: DataFrame.sort_index does fails with `AssertionError`
train.body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3], "foo": [1, 0, 2]}).set_index(["foo"], drop=True)
print(df.sort_index(level="foo"))  # Works in pandas 2 and 3

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3], "foo": [0, 1, 2]}).set_index(["foo"], drop=True)
print(df.sort_index(level="foo"))  # Fails in pandas 3

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3]})
df.index.names = ["foo"]
print(df.sort_index(level="foo"))  # Fails in pandas 2 and 3
```

### Issue Description

From pandas-3.0.0 on the above example fails with
```
     a
foo   
0    1
1    2
2    3
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/tmp/indextest.py", line 8, in <module>
    print(df.sort_index(level="foo"))
          ~~~~~~~~~~~~~^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File "/home/jmu3si/Devel/pandas/pandas/core/frame.py", line 8394, in sort_index
    return super().sort_index(
           ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~^
        axis=axis,
        ^^^^^^^^^^
    ...<7 lines>...
        key=key,
        ^^^^^^^^
    )
    ^
  File "/home/jmu3si/Devel/pandas/pandas/core/generic.py", line 5187, in sort_index
    new_data = self._mgr.take(indexer, axis=baxis, verify=False)
  File "/home/jmu3si/Devel/pandas/pandas/core/internals/managers.py", line 1069, in take
    return self.reindex_indexer(
           ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~^
        new_axis=new_labels,
        ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
    ...<2 lines>...
        allow_dups=True,
        ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
    )
    ^
  File "/home/jmu3si/Devel/pandas/pandas/core/internals/managers.py", line 829, in reindex_indexer
    assert isinstance(indexer, np.ndarray)
           ~~~~~~~~~~^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
AssertionError
```

The issue occurs when the following conditions are met:

* The index is a `RangeIndex`.
* There is only one index level.
* `.sort_index` is called with the `level=` argument.

It feels like kind of a regression because as it seems pandas-2.x ended up with an `Index` in some cases in which pandas-3.x ends up with a `RangeIndex`. So there are cases that worked fine in `pandas-2` which don't in pandas-3.

### Expected Behavior

Up to pandas-2.3.3 this worked and gave the expected output:
```
     a
foo   
0    2
1    1
2    3
     a
foo   
0    1
1    2
2    3
     a
foo   
0    1
1    2
2    3
```

train.title: PERF: datetime index getters functions are 10 times slower with ZoneInfo vs pytz timezone
train.body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the main branch of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

Hello,

Function allowing to get attributes on time index like `.month`, `.year` are 10 times slower when the time index is built from a `ZoneInfo` instead of a `pytz.timezone`.

With pandas 2.2.3, 3.0.1 or from main, with the use of ZoneInfo:
```bash
$ python -m timeit -n 200 -s 'import pandas as pd; from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo' 'pd.date_range("2024-01-01", "2024-12-31 23:59:59", freq="1min", tz=ZoneInfo("Europe/Paris")).month'
200 loops, best of 5: 119 msec per loop
```

With pandas 2.2.3, 3.0.1 or from main with pytz and dztada installed, with the use of pytz timezone:
```bash
$ python -m timeit -n 1000 -s 'import pandas as pd;from pytz import timezone' 'pd.date_range("2024-01-01", "2024-12-31 23:59:59", freq="1min", tz=timezone("Europe/Paris")).month'
1000 loops, best of 5: 11.3 msec per loop
```

Same behavior with `year`, `day`, `hour` and `minute` but I didn't check others.
